#5055. ‘Give It Up’: Saylor Fires Back at Infamous Bitcoin Critic

When American entrepreneur Jeffrey Tucker told Bitcoiners to stop dreaming about Bitcoin becoming the world's most valuable asset, Strategy co-founder Michael Saylor responded with the example of a gold-backed banknote.

"Give it up, Bitcoiners. There is no such thing as money that is not used in exchange," Tucker wrote on X.

Tucker argued that Bitcoiners had brought the criticism upon themselves. They made the mistake of thinking they could simply declare Bitcoin a store of value and that would somehow make it one. That is not how it works, according to Tucker. He argued that nothing in the history of money supports this idea.

In his response, Saylor started with an example involving a bakery. Suppose someone buys bread at a bakery. They pay for the bread with a gold-backed banknote. The baker can use that banknote to pay the miller.  The miller can use it to pay the farmer. All three transactions could be completed using the same banknote, while the gold stays in the vault.

@jeffreytucker Jeffrey, a gold-backed banknote could pay the baker, the miller, and the farmer while the gold stayed in the vault. Today people pay in dollars and save in gold, stocks, and real estate. Bitcoin is competing for those savings.

In the second part of his response, Saylor made an argument familiar to anyone who gets paid in dollars.

Sure, you can use dollars to buy groceries. However, you can still decide to keep some of your wealth in stocks, gold, or real estate.

"Today people pay in dollars and save in gold, stocks, and real estate. Bitcoin is competing for those savings," Saylor wrote.

This last point was less ambitious than the claim Tucker was pushing back against.

Tucker was talking about Bitcoin becoming the world's most valuable asset.

Saylor, meanwhile, was making a simpler argument about where people choose to keep their savings.

However, Saylor's gold analogy raises an interesting question for Tucker. In Saylor's example, gold is still relevant to the purchase of bread because it backs the banknote the baker accepts.

However, in his modern examples, someone who chooses to save in stocks isn't necessarily concerned about whether their local bakery accepts stocks as payment.

For Tucker, it's all about how the customer pays for a loaf of bread. For Saylor, it's about what the baker does with the money after selling it.

#5054. Ethereum’s Co-Founder Takes On Crypto’s Next Security Threat. Who Is Vitalik Buterin?

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

Who is Vitalik Buterin, and why is Ethereum’s co-founder now questioning the security of the very devices crypto investors use to protect their wealth? The 32-year-old programmer has turned his attention to a problem that even open-source software cannot necessarily solve: compromised computer chips.

In an essay published on November 26, Buterin argued that cryptocurrency security needs to extend beyond software and into the physical hardware on which it runs. His message builds on one of crypto’s oldest principles, but with a new twist:

For someone who helped build an alternative to centralized financial infrastructure, questioning the manufacturers behind that infrastructure seems like a natural next step.

Vitalik Buterin is a Russian-Canadian programmer, researcher and writer who conceived Ethereum in 2013, at the age of 19.

Born in Russia in 1994 and raised in Canada, Buterin discovered Bitcoin in 2011. He went on to co-found Bitcoin Magazine, where he explored the technology and economics behind cryptocurrencies long before digital assets attracted mainstream financial institutions.

His involvement in Bitcoin exposed him to a problem that would eventually lead to Ethereum. Blockchain technology had potential beyond transferring money, but building more sophisticated applications on Bitcoin presented technical limitations.

Rather than trying to accommodate every possible application within Bitcoin’s existing architecture, Buterin began working on a blockchain designed specifically for programmability.

At the time, he was studying computer science at the University of Waterloo, where he also worked as a research assistant to cryptographer Ian Goldberg.

According to the University of Waterloo, Buterin received a $100,000 Thiel Fellowship in 2014 and subsequently left university to work on Ethereum full-time.

In November 2013, Buterin wrote the initial draft of what would become the Ethereum whitepaper.

The proposal described a blockchain with a general-purpose programming environment. Developers would no longer need to create an entirely new network every time they wanted to build a decentralized application.

Consider a lending platform. Instead of relying on a bank to manage collateral, calculate interest and authorize withdrawals, developers could encode those rules into smart contracts running on Ethereum.

That does not eliminate every risk. Smart contracts can contain bugs, depend on unreliable external data or operate under centralized administrative controls. What Ethereum introduced was the ability to execute financial and other programmable agreements on a shared blockchain.

Although Buterin originated the concept, Ethereum was not built by him alone. Its founding team included seven other individuals: Gavin Wood, Joseph Lubin, Charles Hoskinson, Anthony Di Iorio, Mihai Alisie, Jeffrey Wilcke and Amir Chetrit.

The project’s first live network, known as Frontier, launched on July 30, 2015.

What began as an experimental computing platform eventually became the foundation for much of the decentralized finance industry. Stablecoins, decentralized exchanges, lending protocols and tokenized financial assets now use the infrastructure that Buterin and Ethereum’s early contributors helped establish.

The network’s own evolution, particularly its transition to proof-of-stake and the development of Layer 2 scaling networks, has shaped Ethereum’s first decade.

A hardware wallet is supposed to keep private keys away from potentially compromised computers and smartphones. But what happens if the device itself cannot be trusted?

Buterin’s latest research examines that possibility. He points to supply chain attacks involving tampered wallets and considers the potential for malicious modifications concealed inside apparently legitimate chips.

Open-source firmware allows researchers to examine the instructions a device runs. But those instructions reveal little about whether the manufactured chip has been altered.

Buterin wants manufacturers to disclose physical chip layouts, known as GDS files, so investigators have a reference against which to inspect actual hardware.

The distinction matters. Knowing what a chip is designed to do is not necessarily the same as knowing what the chip inside your wallet actually does.

One approach highlighted by Buterin comes from hardware security researcher Andrew Huang, better known as bunnie.

Huang has been developing a technique called Infra-Red, In Situ inspection (IRIS), which exploits the fact that silicon becomes transparent at certain infrared wavelengths.

Using infrared illumination and suitable imaging equipment, researchers can examine parts of a chip’s internal structure without necessarily removing it from its circuit board.

The technique could help detect substituted components or unexpected differences between manufactured chips and their intended designs.

In a 2024 update on his research, Huang explained that infrared imaging has resolution limits. It cannot reliably reveal every microscopic feature of modern chips. Combining imaging with additional electrical testing could improve confidence in a component’s integrity.

That is an important limitation for crypto investors. Publishing an open hardware design does not automatically make a wallet secure, just as publishing a smart contract’s code does not establish that it is free of vulnerabilities.

Buterin acknowledges that sophisticated hardware inspections are more likely to be performed by specialist organizations than ordinary wallet owners.

His essay is a proposal for improving security, not an announcement that existing hardware wallets have all been compromised.

Despite his status as Ethereum’s most recognizable co-founder, Buterin is not its CEO.

Ethereum is maintained through the participation of independent developers, researchers, node operators, validators and other ecosystem contributors. Changes to the network involve technical proposals, discussion, software development and adoption by participants.

Buterin has considerable influence over those discussions, but publishing a proposal does not give him the authority to implement it unilaterally.

His role within the Ethereum Foundation is also distinct from control over the blockchain itself. In its April 2025 governance announcement, the Foundation described Buterin’s responsibilities as providing technical and intellectual guidance to the wider ecosystem.

His research can influence the direction Ethereum takes. Whether the network ultimately follows that direction depends on considerably more than his endorsement.

Buterin accumulated considerable wealth through his involvement in Ethereum, with much of his publicly visible cryptocurrency wealth tied to ETH.

However, his exact net worth is not publicly established.

Blockchain analytics can estimate the value of assets held in wallets attributed to him, but those figures do not necessarily account for all his investments, liabilities, private assets or holdings at addresses that have not been publicly identified.

They also fluctuate with cryptocurrency prices. A wallet valuation should therefore not be confused with a complete assessment of his personal wealth.

Buterin’s latest essay is part of a longer-running interest in making digital infrastructure independently verifiable.

In September 2025, he published The Importance of Full-Stack Openness and Verifiability, exploring how transparency could extend across the hardware and software underpinning increasingly important parts of people’s lives.

These interests share a practical concern: whether users can independently establish that the systems they rely on behave as intended.

There is a commercial obstacle, though. Semiconductor manufacturers invest heavily in proprietary processes, and designing chips specifically for inspectability can involve performance compromises.

But a device signing a cryptocurrency transaction does not necessarily need the computing power of a modern AI processor. That makes security-focused hardware a potentially useful starting point.

More than a decade ago, Buterin challenged the idea that blockchains should primarily be used to transfer money. His latest work challenges another assumption the industry has grown comfortable with: that trusting the code is enough.

For crypto investors, the next meaningful development may come from hardware manufacturers willing to make their products independently inspectable, rather than another software update promising greater security.

KuCoin is in the news today after announcing that it would remove Monero [XMR] spot trading on 30th November. The exchange’s XMR/USDT and XMR/USDC pairs accounted for over half of Monero’s spot trading volume on CoinGecko.

With such a large trading venue leaving, where would Monero traders go next?

KuCoin has scheduled the removal of XMR/USDT, XMR/USDC, XMR/ETH and XMR/BTC for 08:00 UTC on 30th November. Deposits have already been closed permanently too.

Withdrawals will close at 08:00 UTC on 31st December 2026. KuCoin reserves the right to close them earlier over project-related issues, with the exchange also warning that stablecoin conversion of remaining balances won’t be guaranteed.

At press time, CoinGecko highlighted $90.42 million in combined 24-hour volumes across KuCoin’s XMR/USDT and XMR/USDC pairs. Together, they accounted for 50.27% of Monero’s spot trading volume.

Including XMR/BTC and XMR/ETH, that brought KuCoin’s total to $104.60 million or 58.14%.

Hence, the question: Where could that trading move now? At the time of writing, the remaining exchanges showed more buy orders close to the market price, despite reporting a lower turnover.

Kraken’s XMR/USD pair had approximately $386,970 in buy orders within 2% below its price, compared to KuCoin’s XMR/USDT pair’s $85,683. WhiteBIT and HTX’s XMR/USDT pairs showed $260,810 and $196,231, respectively.

That gave Kraken roughly 4.5 times KuCoin’s nearby buying depth, with WhiteBIT and HTX also offering larger buy-side cushions. These orders could help absorb selling, although traders could cancel them at any time.

That access problem extended into services marketed as alternatives to CEXs.

X user and the founder of XMRHub called KuCoin’s delisting “the most bearish thing for $XMR.” According to the exec, the exchange supported swap services, liquidity, and onboarding.

Another X user, PerpetualCow, described the alleged connection more directly. He said,

Instant swap exchanges don’t have their own liquidity, they simply wrapped around Kucoin and sold/bought into their order books.

Still, the proposed dependency might explain why another exchange closure could affect apparently separate services. Swap interface routing orders through KuCoin would need another supplier, sufficient inventory, or a different execution route.

Dash’s Joel Valenzuela also raised a similar concern. He warned that further CEX losses could make no-KYC Monero swaps harder to obtain.

Finally, Cake Wallet founder Vik Sharma also directed users towards wallet-based swaps, writing,

Why does Monero keep getting delisted? Because it works!

The announcement followed another loss of exchange access earlier that month. MEXC ended XMR spot trading on 17th November. Its XMR Perpetual Futures closed separately on 13th November.

Kraken, for its part, had been explicit about its own rationale. It cited regulatory changes when halting XMR trading and deposits for European Economic Area customers on 31st October 2024.

It is JPMorgan's willingness to spend money serving Bitcoin clients that tells us more about its plans than CEO Jamie Dimon calling the cryptocurrency a "pet rock."

Scaramucci also claimed that a research note circulating within JPMorgan's private bank recommended allocating 10% of a portfolio to Bitcoin, describing it as potentially the most undervalued asset of the next decade.

The American financier did not provide a timeline for the spending estimate. Neither the estimate nor the research note could be independently verified through publicly available JPMorgan documents.

Scaramucci was referring to what it might cost JPMorgan to develop a business serving Bitcoin clients.

The 10% allocation recommendation, meanwhile, concerns how much of a client's portfolio should be invested in Bitcoin.

If you have a $1 million portfolio, that would mean allocating $100,000 to Bitcoin.

It doesn't mean JPMorgan is buying Bitcoin and adding it to its own balance sheet.

There is a specific example of what JPMorgan already offers in a securities filing dated Nov. 24.

The filing covers $300,000 worth of notes linked to BlackRock's iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF, priced by JPMorgan's financing subsidiary.

Someone who invests $1,000 in these notes could receive $1,300 if the ETF closes at or above its initial price on the observation date in November 2027.

Scaramucci suggested that Dimon has regulators in mind when he publicly criticizes Bitcoin.

However, he also made it clear that customers could buy Bitcoin and see their holdings reflected on JPMorgan statements. At the time, he said the bank would leave custody to third parties.

"I defend your right to buy Bitcoin," Dimon said.

#5050. Zcash Developers Race to Secure Crypto. Can Quantum Computing Break Bitcoin?

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

Can quantum computing break crypto? For years, the question has largely been treated as a problem for the distant future. Zcash developers, however, are already discussing what to do with hundreds of thousands of coins that could become vulnerable if certain cryptographic protections fail.

A day earlier, Shielded Labs published its first technical update on a separate project designed to protect Zcash against future quantum computers.

Neither development means cryptocurrency has been cracked. Together, however, they raise a more pressing question: can blockchain developers replace the mathematics protecting investors’ money before someone finds a way around it?

Quantum computing is a way of processing information using the properties of quantum mechanics. Unlike conventional computers, which represent information using bits with a value of either zero or one, quantum computers operate using quantum bits, commonly known as qubits.

By manipulating these qubits, researchers can design algorithms capable of solving certain mathematical problems far more efficiently than conventional computers.

The important word here is certain. A quantum computer is not simply a faster version of the laptop sitting on your desk. Its advantages depend on the type of problem it is trying to solve.

Unfortunately for the cryptocurrency industry, some of those problems underpin the security of digital wallets.

As explained in NewsBTC’s guide to quantum computing, blockchains rely on cryptographic signatures to establish ownership and authorize transactions. A sufficiently powerful quantum computer could undermine some of the signature systems currently used to protect digital assets.

When you send Bitcoin from your wallet, the network needs to establish that you have the authority to spend those coins. It does this by verifying a digital signature produced using your private key.

Your private key is supposed to remain secret. The corresponding public key can be disclosed because working backward from a public key to its private counterpart is computationally impractical using conventional methods.

In 1994, mathematician Peter Shor introduced a quantum algorithm that could efficiently solve certain mathematical problems underlying modern public-key cryptography.

A sufficiently powerful quantum computer running such an algorithm could potentially recover private keys from exposed public keys. An attacker could then create a transaction that the blockchain would recognize as valid, even though the original owner had never authorized it.

That is a particularly uncomfortable problem for cryptocurrencies. Bitcoin does not have a customer service department that can reverse an unauthorized transfer.

The National Institute of Standards and Technology has already developed alternative cryptographic standards intended to withstand these future attacks. The challenge for crypto is incorporating such protection into networks that were originally built around different assumptions.

Bitcoin’s public transaction history makes it possible to estimate how much of its supply could be exposed under certain quantum attack scenarios.

According to a November 25 snapshot from The Quantum Ledger, approximately 7.23 million BTC, representing 35.9% of issued supply under its methodology, was associated with public keys or spending scripts already visible on the blockchain.

Around 1.94 million BTC was classified as exposed because of its output design. A further 5.29 million BTC was associated with addresses that had previously revealed relevant spending information.

Some of these coins date back to Bitcoin’s earliest years, when transactions commonly revealed public keys directly.

Estimates vary between researchers because they do not all measure exposure in exactly the same way. In May 2026, Glassnode’s research identified 6.04 million BTC under its own classification framework.

These figures should not be interpreted as the amount of Bitcoin that will eventually be stolen. They measure a potential vulnerability under a specific future scenario, not an active attack.

Owners of many exposed coins could migrate their holdings if suitable protection becomes available. Dormant wallets whose owners have lost their private keys present a considerably harder problem.

Zcash offers a useful example of how complicated a cryptographic migration can become.

Sapling is one of the network’s older shielded systems. Its proof mechanism relies on mathematical assumptions that Zakura believes warrant additional scrutiny in light of potentially accelerating cryptographic research.

The time to prepare for a cryptographic breakthrough is before it happens.

The amount involved is already changing. A November 27 snapshot from the Zcash Dashboard, timestamped 06:06 UTC, showed approximately 306,684 ZEC remaining in Sapling, below the rounded estimate cited in Zakura’s proposal. The difference does not, by itself, establish that the warning prompted users to move their funds.

The discussion follows Zcash’s recent NU7 network upgrade, which improved transaction speed and continued the network’s transition away from older infrastructure.

Importantly, the immediate concern raised by Zakura is not evidence of a successful quantum attack. It relates to speculative advances in mathematics that could affect particular cryptographic constructions. Those advances remain unverified.

One of the problems its researchers are working on is the size of cryptographic proofs.

Stronger protection can require considerably more data to be processed and transmitted. That can create difficulties for blockchains, where transaction capacity, verification costs and storage requirements already matter.

The team is evaluating two possible approaches and expects to select a direction by the end of January 2027, provided its research progresses as planned.

Ironwood already incorporates features intended to support a future recovery mechanism. However, the developers have made clear that these features do not make Zcash fully quantum-resistant today.

The distinction is important. Having a contingency plan for a future attack is not the same as having protection against one.

Zcash is not the only network confronting these issues.

Bitcoin developers are discussing changes through proposals including BIP-360, which would introduce a transaction output format designed to reduce certain forms of public-key exposure.

A separate draft, BIP-361, explores a gradual transition away from vulnerable signature schemes once suitable alternatives are available.

Neither proposal should be confused with an activated Bitcoin upgrade.

Ethereum faces additional complications. Beyond individual wallets, its security model relies on cryptographic signatures used by validators and other infrastructure.

Ethereum’s quantum-security challenge extends to staking arrangements and institutional custody.

There is also a governance problem that applies particularly to Bitcoin. If millions of coins remain in old wallets that cannot be migrated, should the network eventually restrict their movement to prevent potential theft?

Doing so could protect the broader ecosystem, but it could also prevent legitimate owners from accessing their own money. Leaving those coins untouched carries a different set of risks.

Cryptography alone cannot settle that argument.

There is no reliable date for when a quantum computer capable of breaking widely used cryptocurrency signatures will become available.

Building such a machine requires more than increasing the number of qubits. Those qubits must also be reliable enough to carry out lengthy, complex calculations without errors overwhelming the results.

According to Coinbase Institute’s research, the relevant machines do not yet exist, but the process of upgrading blockchains, wallets and custody infrastructure could itself take years.

For that reason, waiting for an actual attack before implementing stronger cryptography would be a risky approach.

Crypto investors should pay attention to what developers implement, whether wallets support the new protections and whether existing funds can be migrated without compromising ownership.

There is no need to buy a token simply because its developers describe it as quantum-resistant, either. Such claims deserve scrutiny of the underlying cryptography and its implementation.

Zcash’s latest proposals offer a glimpse of the decisions other blockchain communities may eventually face. Replacing an algorithm is one thing. Persuading an entire decentralized financial network to move its money before a deadline is something else entirely.

#5048. BNB Chain’s new blockchain could make the same PancakeSwap trade 27% more expensive

BNB Chain’s proposed gas rules would raise the network fee for a sample PancakeSwap trade by 27% at the same gas price.

On BNB Chain’s proposed network, a trader would pay for all the computing capacity a swap reserves. Applying that rule to one PancakeSwap trade on BNB Smart Chain would raise its network fee by about 27% at the same gas price.

BNB Chain published its new layer-1 litepaper on Nov. 26, describing a separate network being developed alongside BNB Smart Chain (BSC). The design keeps BNB as the gas token, and a public testnet is in preparation.

For trading apps, the proposal pairs early feedback about where a transaction might land with reserved capacity for eligible activity. The devnet bills ordinary transactions for the room they request in a block.

A gas limit is the maximum amount of computing work a transaction can use. On BNB Smart Chain, the network fee for an ordinary transaction reflects the gas it actually uses.

The new devnet orders transactions before execution, using the declared limit to allocate room in the block. An ordinary transaction with a valid sequence number and sufficient funds at execution pays for that full amount, even if it finishes with gas to spare.

On June 26, a successful swap through PancakeSwap’s v3 router used 129,397 gas at 0.05 gwei per unit and paid 0.00000646985 BNB.

At the same price and the same 163,957-gas limit, the new devnet rule would charge 0.00000819785 BNB. The 34,560 units of unused capacity would add 0.000001728 BNB to that one swap’s fee.

At a 150,000-gas limit, the modeled fee would be 0.0000075 BNB, about 16% above the observed BSC fee. At 200,000 gas, it would be 0.00001 BNB, about 55% higher. A router that lowers its limit can save on transactions that fit and still run out of gas when a route takes more work than expected.

A recorded PancakeSwap transaction and the proposed fee rule at the same gas price.

The swap’s recorded limit becomes the billed amount in the model.

Illustrative lower limit, with the original swap’s gas price held constant.

Illustrative higher limit, with the original swap’s gas price held constant.

The proposed rule bills unused gas, so increasing the limit raises the fee even when the swap uses the same amount of gas.

One historical swap. The model holds the effective gas price fixed and applies devnet billing to three declared limits. The alternatives do not establish future network prices or successful execution at those limits.

The June 26, 2026 BSC receipt shows 129,397 gas used and a 163,957 limit at 0.05 gwei. Apply 0.05 gwei to the selected declared limit in the new L1 model. Divide each modeled fee difference by the observed fee and round to the nearest whole percent. Bars show billed gas on a shared 200,000-gas scale.

One historical swap. The model holds the effective gas price fixed and applies devnet billing to three declared limits. The alternatives do not establish future network prices or successful execution at those limits.

An included transaction that meets those conditions still pays the full limit if it reverts or runs out of gas under the devnet fee rules. At execution, an invalid transaction sequence number incurs no gas charge, while insufficient funds can limit what the network collects.

Please enable JavaScript to verify and send this form.

The network’s protected lanes reserve a portion of block capacity for transactions sent to governance-approved contract addresses. A swap sent to an unregistered router cannot use the reservation of a contract that the router calls.

The declared limit counts against a lane’s quota, so a larger buffer also leaves less room for other eligible transactions. Eligible transactions still compete for space within a lane.

The devnet’s preconfirmation documentation lists roughly 20 milliseconds for the block producer to stream a signed update showing a transaction’s intended position.

The transaction’s result is final after execution is committed and the block carrying that commitment has finalized. An app settling a trade needs a successful receipt and must confirm the receipt’s block is on the canonical chain and at or below the execution-finalized height.

A market maker might delay a quote update after seeing that a swap likely to change its reference price has provisional placement.

If the signal prevents costly stale quotes often enough, those savings can cover the recurring charge for unused gas. If the signal is withdrawn, the market maker has to reassess. A router that needs a swap outcome before making its next move still has to wait for execution.

BNB Smart Chain recorded $484.13 million in 24-hour decentralized exchange volume in DefiLlama’s Nov. 27 snapshot.

For any of that activity to move, the proposed network would have to make economic sense for traders at real gas prices. Public testing can show which lanes are available, how often placement signals are withdrawn, and how much spare gas different routes need.

#5044. Ripple CTO Reminds: XRP’s Got No Coercive Mechanism

Home » Ripple (XRP) » Ripple CTO Reminds: XRP’s Got No Coercive Mechanism

David ‘JoelKatz’ Schwartz reminds the crypto crowd that the majority desire still can’t force anyone to play along.

David Schwartz, CTO Emeritus at Ripple and one of the original architects of the XRP Ledger, dropped a clear-eyed reminder on X today about how XRPL consensus actually works.

In response to a community discussion about whether an 80%+ supermajority of nodes could push through a change (in the context of ongoing chatter about Ripple’s large escrow holdings), the famed computer virtuoso JoelKatz spat out:

“If the majority of nodes want something, nothing can stop them from having it. They just can’t force those who don’t agree to go along with them. But the same is true for a minority of nodes too. There’s no coercive mechanism at all.”

David Schwartz’s comment cuts straight to the design philosophy of the XRP Ledger. A group of nodes (even a large majority) can coordinate, run the software they prefer, and activate features among themselves.

What they cannot do is compel every other participant to accept those rules. Dissenting operators simply continue running the version and Unique Node List (UNL) configuration they choose.

No. They'd just disagree with everyone else who didn't want that change and be counted as disagreeing validators, effectively isolating themselves from the network.

The result is either continued coexistence or, if the disagreement is deep enough, a clean split.

This is the same principle that has allowed previous XRPL-related networks to emerge. There is no on-chain “force” button, no automatic override of node operators who decline an update, and no mechanism that lets one side confiscate or rewrite the state of the other side.

The timing is not accidental. Segments of the XRP community have repeatedly floated the idea of burning or otherwise neutralizing large portions of Ripple’s escrowed XRP.

Some have argued that a sufficiently high validator threshold (the ledger currently requires roughly 80% support sustained over two weeks for amendments) should be enough to make such a change binding.

Schwartz’s reply undercuts that assumption: even overwhelming validator support does not create the power to compel non-consenting nodes. Any side that wants different rules must convince node operators to run the code that implements them.

If the majority of nodes want something, nothing can stop them from having it. They just can't force those who don't agree to go along with them. But the same is true for a minority of nodes too. There's no coercive mechanism at all.

Validators coordinate activation; they do not govern the software choices of independent operators.

Schwartz has made versions of this argument for years. Today’s post simply restates it in the face of fresh pressure around escrow and governance. XRP Ledger’s architecture continues to prioritize the absence of coercion over the ability of any group to impose its will on everyone else.

In a nutshell: the majority can have what it wants. It just cannot make the rest of the network come along for the ride.

Ethereum developers have agreed to move ahead with the next step in the Glamsterdam upgrade.

The key takeaway? Reaching consensus was not easy. Developers flagged potential network disruptions and usability issues with the new gas opcode. Still, they decided to proceed with it. In fact, the team also agreed to schedule the Hoodi testnet upgrade for 15th December at 7:12 PM UTC, moving Glamsterdam testing closer to implementation. So, what does this tell us?

As highlighted in the developer’ discussion, Ethereum is emphasizing post-quantum security within its development, in addition to focusing on on-chain enhancements. Simply put, regardless of the ongoing concerns, the developers are clearly moving away from just looking at scaling and speed, and towards ensuring Ethereum is future-proof in relation to quantum computing.

The meeting focused on deciding the scope and timing of the Glamsterdam upgrade and the prioritization of post-quantum security features. The execution layer teams reached a rough consensus to proceed with the current Glamsterdam spec as is, with the Hoodi testnet upgrade scheduled for December 15 at 7:12 PM UTC.

Interestingly, this was also reflected in the debate around the upcoming Heze upgrade.

There was debate about whether to support Fossil or to place a bigger emphasis on post-quantum work. Concern was expressed that Fossil may also require development effort. Though no conclusion was reached, the matter will be discussed further at the next team meeting. Meanwhile, Kevaundray suggested that Keccak256 should be used as the hashing algorithm for Ethereum’s post-quantum work.

Against this backdrop, the Heze upgrade moving forward does not seem far-fetched. With the Hoodi upgrade scheduled and Keccak256 proposed for post-quantum security, Ethereum’s [ETH] focus on strengthening its long-term security is now becoming clearer.

The Hoodi testnet is a testing version of Ethereum that allows developers to trial upcoming upgrades.

Think of it as a testing ground where developers can identify bugs and ensure upgrades like Glamsterdam work smoothly before reaching Ethereum users. Within the wider scope of Ethereum’s post-quantum development, it may also be used to test new security features, again allowing developers to analyze how prepared they are to then apply these to the mainnet.

That makes Hoodi an important test for Glamsterdam, giving developers a clearer picture of whether the upgrade is ready for mainnet. Why does this matter? Well, Glamsterdam aims to improve transaction processing. If successful, these changes could strengthen Ethereum’s network fundamentals. Here, the timing matters too.

As the chart shows, Ethereum has processed just over 100 million transactions in Q4 so far. By comparison, the network averaged more than 200 million transactions per quarter in 2026. This puts Q4 activity well below its recent pace, with ETH’s technical structure also showing signs of weakness.

Against this backdrop, the Hoodi testnet upgrade could mark an important inflection point for Ethereum.

A successful rollout would bring Glamsterdam closer to mainnet deployment. In turn, the upgrade could boost Ethereum’s throughput, improve execution efficiency, and support stronger on-chain activity.

Ethereum developers are moving ahead with Glamsterdam while focusing more on future quantum security.

The Hoodi testnet will help test the upgrade before mainnet, with the goal of making Ethereum faster and more efficient.

Bitcoin whales have reversed their usual year-end pattern. Between September 30 and November 21, balances in addresses holding 1,000 to 10,000 BTC rose by 121,117 BTC even though Bitcoin lost 29.5% of its value. At a reference price of $61,000, those additional coins are worth roughly $7.4 billion.

The figures come from CryptoQuant’s November 27 research report, which was supported by crypto lender CoinRabbit. The study excludes exchange and mining-pool addresses from its balance cohorts. Its findings are a snapshot through November 21, not a final tally for the quarter.

The timing matters. NewsBTC recently reported more than $2 billion in US spot Bitcoin ETF outflows. Fund withdrawals and rising whale balances point in different directions, but they measure different things. Neither tells us whether the same investors are moving their money from ETFs into direct Bitcoin ownership.

A broader measure from Maketo’s whale holdings data puts the balance of addresses with at least 1,000 BTC at 7.22 million BTC on November 26, up 54,379 BTC over the preceding 30 days. That group includes exchange and custody addresses, so it provides a separate view of where coins are held rather than an independent check of CryptoQuant’s 121,117 BTC figure.

The combined balance of the 1,000 to 10,000 BTC cohort at just under 2.95 million BTC on November 21, up from 2.83 million at the end of September.

Large addresses reduced their balances in seven of the nine preceding fourth quarters. Only 2019 and 2020 escaped that pattern. The 4.29% increase recorded so far this quarter is the largest Q4 gain since 2020, although December could still change the result.

For comparison, the cohort lost nearly 203,000 BTC over Q4 2025. This year’s increase has come during a falling market, rather than a rally.

There is a catch in calling this a $7.4 billion accumulation. The figure values the additional coins at a reference price; it does not measure the dollars spent buying them. Transfers between addresses, including movements across the cohort’s balance thresholds, can change the total without a market purchase.

The increase tells us where Bitcoin is sitting. It does not tell us how much fresh capital is behind it. That distinction matters when liquidity is scarce.

The 121,117 BTC figure makes for a bullish headline. The number I would pay closer attention to is the remaining profit margin.

Among addresses holding between 1,000 and 10,000 BTC, the unrealized profit margin fell from 33.9% at the end of September to 5.7% on November 21, its lowest reading of 2026 in the report.

The deterioration is even clearer in dollar terms. Combined unrealized profits for addresses holding at least 1,000 BTC stood at about $24 billion on November 21, down from a peak of $294 billion in August 2025.

Across the broader group of addresses holding at least 1,000 BTC, net realized losses reached approximately $2.1 billion in the first 52 days of Q4. The on-chain data suggests that some large holders are already moving coins at a loss rather than waiting for a recovery.

The relevant distinction is between the balance held at a given date and the profit or loss on coins that move. A growing balance does not prevent other coins within the cohort from being spent below their estimated cost basis.

Exchange deposits deserve a closer look, too. Inflows from unspent transaction outputs (UTXOs) of at least 1,000 BTC averaged 5,012 BTC per day in November through the report’s cutoff, compared with 3,239 in October. That is a measure of large coin outputs, not a count of individual whales.

November’s pickup should not obscure the bigger picture: the quarter-to-date average of 3,955 BTC per day remained below the 2019–2025 Q4 average of 4,575 BTC. Large deposits are not proof of sales, and a rise in this metric alone does not establish that selling pressure has intensified.

The 2018 and 2022 bear markets offer a useful comparison, though not a roadmap for this one.

Balances in the 1,000 to 10,000 BTC cohort declined in both of those fourth quarters. Their average unrealized profit margins were negative, while the group still had a positive margin at the November 21 reading this year.

Today’s accumulation may be a sign that some large holders are willing to retain exposure through the downturn. The address data cannot establish their motives or identify how much of the increase came from new purchases.

I would not call a market bottom on these numbers alone.

A further price decline could wipe out the cohort’s remaining profit cushion. Whether that produces more selling depends on the holders’ liquidity needs and positioning, neither of which can be read directly from address balances.

The next test is whether large-address balances keep rising while net realized losses and large exchange deposits ease. That combination, alongside evidence of renewed spot demand, would make the recovery case more convincing.

For now, the change in year-end positioning is real within CryptoQuant’s measured cohort. Evidence of a durable recovery is still missing.

#5040. Saudi oil shows why the next OPEC+ production increase could deliver less than markets expect

Kuwait was pumping 650,000 barrels a day below its October target, but permission to produce more oil only goes so far when tankers have trouble getting it out.

Saudi Arabia can send oil from its eastern fields to an overseas customer without putting a tanker through the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow passage connecting the Persian Gulf to the open sea. The crude travels by pipeline across the country to Yanbu, a port on the Red Sea, where a ship collects it.

Kuwait, just up the Gulf from those Saudi fields, loads its regular overseas cargoes inside the Gulf, so its tankers have to pass through Hormuz to reach customers beyond it. For a buyer choosing between the two suppliers, that difference can determine how easily an order gets delivered.

Both countries belong to OPEC+, the alliance of oil producers that includes Russia and agrees on how much its members should pump.

Whenever the group meets, an increase in production allowances leads to a pretty straightforward calculation: if you give a country permission to pump another 100,000 barrels a day, buyers should have another 100,000 barrels available to buy.

However, last month's numbers from Kuwait show it's not always such a straightforward case.

The International Energy Agency (IEA) estimated Kuwaiti production at 2.03 million barrels a day against an implied target of 2.68 million, leaving it 650,000 below its allowance. Iraq, another member exporting through Gulf ports, pumped 4.6 million against a target of 4.43 million, putting it 170,000 above.

Kuwait already had permission to produce considerably more oil, and easier shipping could help it sell more without a higher quota. Meanwhile, Iraq could receive a bigger allowance that would bring its target closer to what it was already pumping.

To understand what an OPEC+ agreement buys a producer, it helps to separate the negotiation from the journey to the customer.

Ministers start with a baseline, a reference level from which they calculate a country's production cuts. Applying those cuts produces its target, or the amount it's supposed to pump.

The IEA's implied targets account for voluntary cuts and adjustments to offset earlier overproduction, while its output estimates show how much oil countries actually produced.

Even oil that's been pumped doesn't necessarily become an export cargo. Some goes to domestic refineries, which turn crude into fuels such as diesel and gasoline, and some goes into storage.

The amount left for overseas buyers still needs a way to reach a port and a ship that can complete the voyage.

Saudi Arabia pumped 9.99 million barrels a day in October against an implied target of 10.48 million, according to the IEA. Separately, the US Energy Information Administration estimated that the Hormuz disruption took roughly 500,000 barrels a day of Saudi production offline, compared with 560,000 in Kuwait and 60,000 in Iraq.

Those estimates measure production lost to the disruption, so they measure something different from the gap between output and an OPEC+ target. Iraq could lose output at some fields because oil couldn't get out, even while still producing more nationwide than its OPEC+ target allowed.

October 2026 production minus the IEA's implied OPEC+ target, in thousand barrels a day. Below zero: production below target. Above zero: production above target. Kuwait produced 2.03 million barrels a day against a 2.68 million target; Saudi Arabia produced 9.99 million against 10.48 million; Iraq produced 4.60 million against 4.43 million.

Source: International Energy Agency, Oil Market Report, November 2026; October estimates cited in the article

Saudi Arabia has an advantage in recovering that lost business because its East-West Pipeline carries oil from Abqaiq, near the eastern fields, across the kingdom to Yanbu. Saudi Aramco reported capacity of 7 million barrels a day earlier this year, including about 2 million for refineries.

Please enable JavaScript to verify and send this form.

Oil delivered to a Saudi refinery may eventually be exported as diesel, but a foreign refinery buying crude needs barrels it can process itself.

The EIA attributed part of October's export recovery to the pipeline's restart, showing how restoring a route can get more oil to customers. Aramco has also begun preliminary engineering for an expansion, though it offers no extra capacity for cargo booked today.

Kuwait's usual maritime crude exports still depart from inside the Gulf, and the region's bypass pipelines give it no comparable direct route. Its buyers must allow for passage through Hormuz even when Kuwait has ample room under its production target.

Iraq does have a pipeline to the Mediterranean through Turkey, but the northern route serves a different set of fields from those around Basra, whose oil normally leaves through southern Gulf ports.

Diverting those southern exports would require a physical connection to the northern route and the right to use it. Access to an export pipeline also doesn't automatically entitle a producer to load whatever cargo it chooses.

In October, northern producer ShaMaran said Iraq's state oil marketer had allocated an additional cargo to international producers, partly to settle money owed for oil sold in 2025. Getting paid depended in part on who was allowed to load the ship.

Within the Gulf, shippers have adapted by using smaller tankers to carry crude out for transfer to larger vessels, according to the EIA's November freight analysis. Shipments of crude and condensate, a light liquid often produced alongside natural gas, through Hormuz recovered from 3.8 million barrels a day in the second quarter to 7.3 million in the third.

That was still only about 46% of the 15.9 million passing through in the last quarter of 2025, although it understates the region's total exports because Saudi cargoes loaded at Yanbu never enter the strait.

This helps explain how attacks on tankers in Hormuz can disrupt individual voyages while more of the region's oil reaches buyers.

The EIA estimated that production taken offline across the region fell from 10.9 million barrels a day in May to 2.54 million in October. Iran accounted for 1.08 million barrels in October, roughly 43%, although it doesn't participate in the seven-country agreement on voluntary production adjustments. Much of the oil still held back by the disruption therefore falls outside that agreement.

When those seven producers last met, on Nov. 1, they kept December's targets at September levels. The wider alliance is also assessing production capacity for its 2027 baselines, which will help determine how future cuts are divided.

A higher baseline could give a country a larger allowance in a future deal without adding a single cargo to next month's exports.

For investors watching oil's contribution to inflation and the interest rates that feed into Bitcoin trading, the previous quota decision offered an example of how supply can improve under unchanged targets.

Recovering exports helped bring crude prices down while those targets held steady. The journey also affects how much reassurance to take from a buildup in stocks: oil aboard a ship and oil already on land can both count toward inventories, but only one has completed its sea voyage.

Refiners buying Saudi crude get a better answer from the loading port on their offer. If it's Yanbu, the crude reaches the ship by pipeline across Saudi Arabia, letting the tanker load it without entering the Gulf.

That route gives the buyer something a larger production allowance alone can't promise: a cargo that can reach them without passing through Hormuz.

XRP is on track for its worst November on record and has lost 48.3% in 2026 so far. The token also ended 2014, 2018 and 2022 with annual losses.

CryptoRank data shows that XRP has lost 24% in November so far, as of Friday. Before 2026, the token's worst November was in 2019, when it lost 23.3%. The month will close on Monday, Nov. 30.

According to CryptoRank, XRP's high for 2026 was $2.40, and its low was $0.87 in November. In the fourth quarter, the token has lost 36.1% so far, and in 2026, XRP has lost value in seven of 11 months so far. On Friday, XRP rose as high as $0.987 on Binance and was trading at around $0.95 later in the day, up 0.5%, according to TradingView.

Veteran trader Peter Brandt has also used the four-year cycle in his forecasts for Bitcoin. In April 2026, Brandt said that if the cycle holds, Bitcoin's next peak could come in September or October 2029 at $300,000 to $500,000.

In 2014, XRP lost 10.7% over the year, but the token gained 130.4% in November and 118.1% in December, according to CryptoRank.

In 2018, XRP lost 84.5% over the year. The token also lost 19.3% and 2.25% in November and December of that year, respectively. In 2022, the annual loss was 59.2%, and XRP lost 11.8% in November and 16.9% in December.

XRP's median December return is -4.07%, and its average December return is 63.1%, according to CryptoRank data. In December 2017, XRP gained 818.9%. The token closed December in the red in eight of the past 13 years, including December 2025, when it lost 14.8%.

XRP's largest December loss came in 2020. The token lost 66.5% that month, after the SEC sued Ripple on Dec. 22, 2020.

XRP ended 2015 with a 75.3% loss and 2019 with a 47.1% loss, according to CryptoRank. In 2023, the token gained 82.5%.

In the first quarter of 2015, XRP lost 68.2%. The token lost 12.8% in the first quarter of 2019 and gained 58.8% in the first quarter of 2023.

On Dec. 1, Ripple's escrow will unlock another 1 billion XRP.

The SingleAssetVault amendment on the XRP Ledger reached a majority on Nov. 25. According to XRPScan, it can activate as early as Dec. 9 at 7:38 p.m. UTC.

According to Ripple, lenders will deposit funds into a Single Asset Vault, and loan brokers will use that capital to issue loans and track repayments on the ledger.

On Friday, the LendingProtocolV1_1 amendment reached 29 of 35 validator votes, according to XRPScan. Its earliest activation date is Dec. 11 at 2:22 p.m. UTC, and its support has to stay above 80% until then.

#5038. HBAR Tokenization Lags The Headlines, Price Tests Support

Home » Trendsetter News » HBAR Tokenization Lags The Headlines, Price Tests Support

With publicly tracked assets below $100 million, sustained network usage and rising fee revenue remain key signals to watch.

Hedera has less than $100 million in publicly tracked tokenized assets despite its institutional announcements and industry awards, according to a crypto analyst examining HBAR’s retreat toward five cents. The video’s central argument: recognition has not yet translated into enough network activity or token demand to support the price.

At the time of recording, HBAR was roughly 90% below its September 2021 high near $0.57, back around the levels preceding its late-2024 rally. The analyst recalls a move from approximately four cents to more than 30 cents in about a month, but cautions that the ETF filing associated with that rally is no longer a fresh catalyst.

Fire Hustle highlights Hedera’s Digital Assets Award at the 2026 US FinTech Awards and the addition of Apex Group to its governing council. Apex oversees more than $3.5 trillion in assets, according to the video.

There is an important qualification. Apex had only said it would explore using Hedera, while its main tokenization project was being built on the Polygon-based T-REX Ledger.

“None of it forces anyone to buy HBAR,” the analyst says.

Citing RWA.xyz, the video puts Hedera’s publicly tracked, holdable and tradable tokenized assets below $100 million, compared with more than $600 million on the XRP Ledger. It also cites Stellar’s reported tokenized assets approaching $4 billion, although those figures should not automatically be treated as identical measures.

The YouTube video reports roughly 500,000 daily Hedera transactions, or six to seven per second, and network fees of only a few hundred dollars a day. Fees are denominated in dollars but paid in HBAR; network usage does not burn the token.

Those mechanics matter: higher transaction counts alone do not establish substantial buying pressure.

Fire Hustle wants sustained activity, rising fee revenue, stronger ETF inflows and a broader rotation into altcoins before treating the headlines as evidence of improving investment fundamentals.

On the chart, five cents is the first area to hold. Fire Hustle would consider staggered limit orders around three to four cents if weakness deepens, while reclaiming seven cents would be an early sign that selling pressure is easing, not proof of a durable recovery.

With Bitcoin (BTC) dominance near 60%, the investment hurdle is relative performance: HBAR must justify its additional risk against Bitcoin, not merely recover in dollar terms.

#5036. CZ Alerts Crypto Apps to Warn iPhone Users About DarkSword

Amid the recurring security threats facing crypto users, especially iOS users, Binance’s founder Changpeng Zhao has sent a cautionary notice to not just crypto users but also to platforms providing crypto services via mobile apps.

CZ’s warnings come amid ongoing security concerns about an increase in DarkSword attacks targeting iPhone users with outdated iOS versions.

The attack poses massive risks to crypto users as it serves as an iOS exploit kit that hits unpatched phones on versions from 18.4 to 18.7, putting them at risk of losing their funds.

The viral DarkSword attack has caused Binance to roll out security warnings via its application, alerting users running vulnerable versions of Apple's iOS.

In a recent X post, CZ explained that users running affected iOS versions, specifically iOS 18.4 through 18.7, will see security alerts across its ecosystem, especially on Binance apps and websites, to allow detection of the operating system.

He mentioned that the warnings will appear on platforms and services, including Trust Wallet, CoinMarketCap, PancakeSwap, BNB Chain, and Binance Wallet.

To keep users informed and cautious, the alert will notify users that their iOS versions may be vulnerable to DarkSword attacks. It will also inform them of the risk involved, as the attack could expose sensitive information when they visit malicious websites.

Furthermore, Binance advised iPhone users to update to the latest available iOS version to reduce potential security risks.

To further hedge against potential threats, users are also given the option to view instructions on how to update their devices.

Given the rise in the acceptance of digital assets, the ASEAN+3 member countries have agreed to establish a dedicated working group to advance discussions on cross-border digital payments and regulatory approaches to digital assets.

The decision was announced in the Co-chairs’ Statement following the ASEAN+3 Finance and Central Bank Deputies’ Meeting held in Kyoto, Japan recently.

Here, the initiative aims to strengthen regional financial cooperation by improving payment connectivity and encouraging discussions on how crypto should be regulated across participating economies.

In fact, it also marks a step towards greater coordination among Asian financial authorities as digital assets and blockchain-based financial services continue to expand.

To make this successful, the proposed working group aims to operate under the newly established AMRO Cross-Border Digital Payments Program. Under the same, they will provide a dedicated platform for ASEAN+3 economies to discuss retail and wholesale payment connectivity, alongside regulatory approaches to digital assets.

This is particularly important because cross-border payments remain fragmented across different financial systems. Needless to say, differences in payment infrastructure, regulations, and compliance requirements make international transactions slower and more expensive.

However, with greater coordination, participating economies could explore inter-operable payment systems and more consistent regulatory approaches.

Interestingly, the development also comes amid broader efforts by governments and financial regulators to address the growing influence of cryptocurrencies, stablecoins, and tokenized assets.

One prominent example is the European Union’s Markets in Crypto-Assets (MiCA) framework. It became fully applicable on 30th December 2024, following the introduction of stablecoin-specific provisions in June 2024.

For those unaware, MiCA establishes common rules for crypto-asset issuers and service providers, covering authorization, transparency, investor protection, and market conduct. Its implementation has provided a regulatory benchmark for other jurisdictions considering comprehensive crypto frameworks.

South Africa is another example of this shift. In August 2026, the South African Reserve Bank (SARB) and National Treasury proposed an activity-based reporting framework for cross-border crypto transactions.

The proposal focuses on identifying and monitoring transactions that could facilitate capital flight, illegal financial flows, or regulatory circumvention. Rather than classifying crypto assets as official currency, it seeks to bring their cross-border movement under closer financial safeguards.

On the other hand, the United States has faced setbacks in establishing similar regulatory clarity. The proposed Digital Asset Market CLARITY Act failed to advance in the Senate on 15th September, receiving 49 votes in favor and 50 against. it was short of the 60 votes required to proceed.

Its failure has left the U.S without the proposed comprehensive federal market structure framework, potentially putting it behind jurisdictions such as the E.U in providing regulatory certainty. However, the SEC and CFTC continue to pursue regulatory initiatives under their existing authority.

Against this backdrop, ASEAN+3’s latest decision is the latest in the world’s global regulatory discussion/efforts.

#5034. Vitalik Buterin warns against rushing Ethereum gas change that could break some contracts

Developers are keeping Glamsterdam’s gas changes and targeting a Dec. 15 test while affected apps work on fixes.

Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin has warned against rushing the Glamsterdam upgrade because its new gas rules could break some existing smart contracts. Developers are targeting Dec. 15 for a testnet activation.

In a Nov. 28 post on X, Buterin acknowledged that complaints about Ethereum Improvement Proposal (EIP) 8037 breaking existing smart contracts were valid, even though he considered the changes necessary for Ethereum's long-term sustainability.

Buterin argued that changes to fundamental aspects of the blockchain could undermine confidence in immutable smart contracts by encouraging application developers to give administrators greater control over deployed code.

“We do NOT want an Ethereum where it becomes ‘prudent security advice' to have centralized upgrade hatches ‘just in case'.”

The Ethereum co-founder urged core developers to assume responsibility for supporting applications disrupted by network upgrades. He also called on the Ethereum Foundation, Ethlabs and other ecosystem organizations to expand their efforts to help affected developers.

“Given its breaking nature, Glamsterdam should not be rushed.”

At their Nov. 26 meeting, Ethereum core developers agreed to keep Glamsterdam’s existing gas pricing rules and targeted Dec. 15 at 19:12 UTC for activation on the Hoodi testnet.

The decision followed weeks of deliberations after the Ethereum Foundation postponed the Oct. 26 Hoodi test over smart contract compatibility concerns.

During the Nov. 26 meeting, execution-layer client teams declined to block the existing specifications despite lingering reservations. Consensus-layer developers also settled on a solution for validating block builders' execution payloads, clearing another technical obstacle to the Hoodi deployment.

Client teams are targeting software releases for the week beginning Nov. 30, ahead of Glamsterdam's final public testnet activation.

Glamsterdam represents a major step in Ethereum's ambition to expand its base-layer capacity following the Fusaka upgrade.

The upgrade changes how Ethereum constructs and validates blocks and lays the groundwork for parallel transaction processing and a 200 million block gas limit, up from 60 million.

Please enable JavaScript to verify and send this form.

Blockchain analytics platform Growthepie estimates that the increase could raise Ethereum's layer-1 throughput from 24.9 transactions per second (TPS) to approximately 80 TPS in early 2027.

That additional capacity could allow Ethereum to accommodate substantially more decentralized finance activity, stablecoin payments, and institutional settlements directly on its mainnet.

However, expanding the gas limit without changing how Ethereum prices network resources could accelerate the growth of its permanent database, increasing hardware requirements for node operators.

EIP-8037 addresses this problem by raising the gas cost of creating new accounts, storage entries, and smart contract code. A related proposal, EIP-8038, adjusts the cost of accessing existing network state.

The changes could cause some smart contracts to exhaust gas allowances that previously covered their operations.

A Nov. 18 impact assessment by ChainSecurity, alongside investigations coordinated by the Ethereum Foundation, documented 200 compatibility findings, including three classified as high severity.

The affected systems include bridges, wallets, exchanges, staking protocols, and governance mechanisms, with potential consequences ranging from interrupted operations to locked funds and incorrect reward calculations.

While configuration changes can resolve most findings, 24 require contract upgrades or migrations.

On Nov. 25, Ethereum research organization Ethlabs recommended retaining Glamsterdam's existing specifications, arguing that removing EIP-8037 would sacrifice the planned threefold increase in the gas limit.

The organization added that modifying the proposal would resolve only some compatibility issues while introducing several months of additional development work.

Meanwhile, the Ethereum Foundation and its research partners have contacted more than 50 affected companies to coordinate remediation efforts.

According to Ethereum Institutional, the most severely affected projects have either implemented fixes or expect to complete them by mid-December, while others expect to be ready by Jan. 10.

Developers have identified mid-January 2027 as the earliest possible Glamsterdam mainnet window, although late January or early February appears more realistic. No mainnet activation date has been agreed upon.

The countdown to Bitcoin's next halving continues, with exactly 500 days remaining until the network's fifth scheduled supply reduction, expected in April 2028.

About every four years, the reward that Bitcoin pays for mining a block is cut in half. Bitcoin's community-run website, bitcoin.org, tracks the countdown to the next halving and reports 72,073 blocks left until the next halving event.

The next halving is expected to take place at block height 1,050,000, reducing the Bitcoin mining reward from 3.125 BTC to 1.5625 BTC per block.

Bitcoin targets the creation of one block every 10 minutes on average, so the date of block 1,050,000 can only be estimated. Blocks tend to arrive slightly faster when mining power grows; thus, halvings might arrive a little earlier than a simple calendar estimate.

New Bitcoins enter circulation as a reward to the miner of each block. Every 210,000 blocks, which is about four years, that reward is cut in half in the halving event. It started at 50 Bitcoins per block in 2009 and will reach zero around the year 2140, when all Bitcoins will have been issued.

The halving countdown remains significant, as Bitcoin has typically traded in a four-year price cycle centered around the event.

The last halving took place in April 2024, and the one before that was in May 2020. There was an unprecedented market reaction around the last halving as Bitcoin hit a high above $73,000 in March 2024, about a month before the halving, rather than reaching new heights after the celebrated event as expected.

Bitcoin is trading at $59,269, down more than 53% from its all-time high of more than $126,000 in October 2025. Bitcoin traded as high as $97,915.90 in January of this year before it declined. The broader digital asset market has struggled after the Clarity Act, a crypto market structure bill, failed to advance in the Senate in September.

According to Glassnode, buyers have built a floor under BTC. After the slide toward $55,000, a dense cluster of bids has formed between $50,000 and $58,000, with support this strong, which was last seen in August 2026. Breaking through it would require aggressive selling pressure.

#5031. Trump Crypto News: World Liberty Financial Sells $20 Million in Ethereum Assets, Data Shows

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

Trump-backed crypto project World Liberty Financial has reportedly reduced its Ethereum exposure by approximately $20 million, converting two large holdings into dollar-pegged stablecoins during the latest cryptocurrency market downturn.

Blockchain monitoring platform Lookonchain reported that a wallet associated with the project sold 10,600 ETH and 1,378 mETH, receiving approximately $20.06 million.

Separate estimates from on-chain analyst Ember suggest the assets may have been sold at a loss of more than $19 million.

The transactions come just weeks after World Liberty Financial announced a WLFI token buyback program, which could be partly funded by income generated from its USD1 stablecoin reserves.

The Ethereum sales represent a notable reversal for a project that previously accumulated the cryptocurrency during periods of market weakness. Where the money went, however, deserves just as much attention as what was sold.

The reported transactions involved approximately $17.58 million in USDC and another $2.48 million in USD1, World Liberty Financial’s own dollar-pegged stablecoin.

Transaction records from Arkham show a series of transfers between World Liberty Financial’s labeled Strategic Reserve wallet and CoW Protocol, involving outgoing mETH and incoming USD1. The wallet also interacted with decentralized lending protocol Dolomite.

The Ethereum assets included wrapped ether, known as WETH, and mETH, a token representing exposure to staked Ethereum.

The latter distinction matters because a liquid staking token does not necessarily trade at a one-to-one ratio with ETH. Simply adding the number of WETH and mETH tokens together can give a misleading picture of the underlying Ethereum exposure.

According to Ember’s estimates, the combined holdings represented approximately 12,121 ETH in equivalent exposure.

The analyst estimated an average acquisition cost of $3,244 per ETH, compared with an average disposal value of approximately $1,655.

If that cost-basis estimate is accurate, the transactions would represent a loss of roughly $19.26 million, or close to half the original investment.

World Liberty Financial’s reported Ethereum sale. Cost basis and loss are on-chain estimates, not audited results. Data: Lookonchain, Ember. Visualization: NewsBTC.

World Liberty Financial has not been shown to have confirmed that loss in a public accounting statement. The figure remains an on-chain estimate rather than an audited financial result.

World Liberty Financial’s decision to move part of the reported proceeds into USD1 raises questions beyond the performance of its Ethereum investments.

In its official USD1 risk disclosures, World Liberty Financial acknowledges that its financial interests and those of BitGo may differ from those of USD1 holders. Both benefit from net fees earned through interest on the stablecoin’s reserves, while USD1 holders are not entitled to those earnings.

That makes USD1 more than another cryptocurrency held in the project’s treasury. It is part of the business through which World Liberty Financial seeks to generate revenue from its digital-dollar product.

Holding USD1, however, does not automatically generate a return for the wallet that receives it. Nor does an exchange of existing tokens necessarily increase the stablecoin’s circulating supply or reserve income.

The relevant question is whether the transactions represent temporary treasury management or a broader change in the project’s investment strategy.

In January, NewsBTC reported that World Liberty Financial had acquired approximately 2,868 ETH after selling more than $8 million worth of wrapped Bitcoin.

The November transactions point in the opposite direction, with the reported wallet moving away from Ethereum-linked exposure and toward dollar-denominated assets.

It would nevertheless be misleading to conclude that World Liberty Financial has abandoned Ethereum entirely. The activity concerns a specific wallet, and the project’s broader holdings across other addresses have not been established by these transactions.

Data from Arkham Intelligence shows that the project’s labeled Strategic Reserve wallet held approximately $243.8 million in digital assets on November 28. Notably, more than 96% of that valuation came from its own WLFI token, while the wallet retained 2,000 ETH worth approximately $3.32 million.

The concentration raises a separate question about the reserve’s exposure to fluctuations in the price of its own token. Its reported portfolio value should not necessarily be confused with readily available liquidity.

There is also no verified evidence that President Donald Trump personally instructed the trades.

For Ethereum investors, the reported sale is another example of a large crypto-linked entity reducing exposure during a difficult market. For World Liberty Financial’s stakeholders, the more consequential questions concern its treasury strategy, the management of investment losses and the transparency of its financial disclosures.

The blockchain can reveal how assets moved. It cannot, on its own, explain who authorized those movements or why.

#5029. Vitalik Buterin Defends Ethereum’s EIP-8037 Despite Contract Loophole

Vitalik Buterin, the cofounder of the leading blockchain network, Ethereum, has defended the proposed EIP-8037 upgrade on the blockchain despite growing concerns that the change could break some existing smart contracts.

In a recent post shared on X on November 28, Buterin did not dismiss these concerns, echoing developers' concerns even as the upgrade continues to draw near.

Although the Ethereum founder acknowledged that developers affected by the proposal have legitimate reasons to raise concerns, he has maintained his belief that the changes are necessary to help stabilize Ethereum in the long term.

He further warned against centralized upgrade hatches, advising that Ethereum should not become a network where developers are encouraged to build centralized upgrade mechanisms into their applications as a precaution against future protocol changes.

To back his advice, Buterin mentioned possible consequences, noting that when such practices are allowed and become normalized, they could introduce unexpected centralization risks into the broader Ethereum ecosystem.

Despite standing by the implementation of the Ethereum EIP-8037 upgrade, Buterin acknowledged that the potential contract breakage threats posed by the upgrade should also be taken into consideration.

He urged that breaking existing applications should not be treated as an easy or routine consequence of Ethereum's development process. Hence, he charged core developers with the responsibility to support application developers whose projects are affected by protocol changes, especially when those developers had reasonable grounds to believe certain aspects of Ethereum would remain unchanged.

As such, Buterin praised the Ethereum Foundation, ETH Labs, and others for their contributions in helping application developers navigate the necessary upgrades.

The simultaneous selloff has raised questions about World Liberty Financial's treasury movements and governance token-backed borrowing positions.

World Liberty Financial, the crypto project backed by President Donald Trump's family, suffered a sharp market selloff on Nov. 28 as its WLFI governance token plunged nearly 60% and its USD1 stablecoin lost its dollar peg.

CryptoSlate data shows that WLFI fell to a record low of $0.01718 before recovering to $0.02033. The selloff accelerated during a 14-minute period, when the token plunged 40% from $0.035 to $0.021.

The decline wiped hundreds of millions of dollars from WLFI's market capitalization, which fell from $1 billion to $557 million before recovering to $667 million.

Meanwhile, USD1 traded as low as $0.9487, falling more than 5% below its intended dollar peg before recovering toward $0.98.

The depeg compounded a monthlong contraction in USD1's market capitalization, which fell by about $1 billion, or 26%, from $3.8 billion to $2.8 billion.

The market turmoil followed a series of unusual transactions involving World Liberty Financial's strategic reserve, decentralized lending protocol Dolomite, and crypto exchange Gate.

Blockchain analyst Specter reported that World Liberty's strategic reserve sold 10,600 wrapped Ethereum (WETH) and 1,378 Mantle Staked Ether (mETH) for approximately $17.58 million in USDC and $2.5 million in USD1.

The reserve subsequently deposited $16.9 million in USDC and $2.5 million in USD1 into Dolomite, which powers World Liberty Financial's lending and borrowing platform. Hours later, Dolomite's Margin contract transferred 24 million USD1 to a Gate deposit address across seven transactions, leaving the contract with just $208,000 worth of the stablecoin.

Specter described the sequence of transactions as suspicious.

The transactions have intensified scrutiny of World Liberty Financial's practice of using its own governance token as collateral to borrow stablecoins through Dolomite.

Saturday's selloff threatens to weaken the collateral backing any outstanding WLFI-denominated borrowing positions, potentially forcing borrowers to provide additional assets or repay their debts to avoid liquidation.

Against this backdrop, Tron founder Justin Sun, one of World Liberty Financial's earliest major investors, accused the project of engaging in circular lending to extract liquidity, unauthorized insider selling, unlawfully freezing investor assets, and defrauding investors.

Sun urged crypto exchanges to delist WLFI and USD1 and restrict deposits of both tokens. He also called on regulators and judicial authorities to investigate the movement of funds associated with the project.

The billionaire further alleged that individuals associated with World Liberty Financial had begun deleting social media posts and communications to conceal their activities.

Sun's accusations mark the latest escalation in a months-long dispute over World Liberty Financial's decision to restrict access to his WLFI holdings, which has prompted legal action from both parties.
