#5027. XRP Lending Nearly Activated After Voting Breakthrough

Home » Trendsetter News » XRP Lending Nearly Activated After Voting Breakthrough

An XRP Ledger lending proposal has reached the 80% validator-support threshold, bringing native credit markets closer.

An XRP Ledger lending proposal has reportedly crossed the validator-support threshold needed to move toward activation, potentially adding native credit markets to the network.

In a market-update video, Avi Lev highlighted the development while XRP traded near $0.94 following a broader crypto sell-off.

The proposal, identified in the transcript as XLS-66, would introduce lending directly on the ledger rather than through external smart contracts. The host reported 29 supporting votes and cited commentary saying the amendment had reached the required 80% threshold.

The timing matters. Lev initially suggested a 30-day waiting period, then read a statement attributed to XRP advocate and lawyer John Deaton specifying that support must hold for two weeks before activation. The video therefore describes a conditional milestone, not an already operational lending service.

Under the model outlined in the YouTube episode, lenders would place assets in shared vaults to earn yield, while borrowers would receive fixed-rate, fixed-term loans.

Credit assessments would happen off-chain, with loan disbursements and repayments recorded on-chain.

“This makes it a credit market, too,” read the statement attributed to Deaton. For investors, that is the central development: another potential use for assets on the ledger, though the video offered no lending-volume projections or evidence of resulting demand for XRP.

The lending discussion followed a difficult Black Friday session. According to the host’s chart commentary, XRP fell from roughly $0.96, dropping about 3.6% over approximately 44 minutes after U.S. stock trading opened. Bitcoin lost around 4% in a similar window.

Avi Lev blamed thin holiday liquidity, leveraged liquidations and possible options-related positioning. Claims that ETFs or market makers deliberately pushed prices lower were interpretations.

Separately, Avi Lev a.k.a Money Maker cited a reported 53% plunge in a Trump-family-linked World Liberty Financial token over 60 minutes, alongside reports that a linked wallet sold 12,000 ETH. The cause remained unclear.

The distinction is between a possible expansion in network utility and immediate price performance. Lending activation would be worth monitoring, but the session described in the video showed XRP still moving closely with the wider market.

Solana developers have issued an urgent instruction to network operators, asking them to install the latest version of the Agave validator client without delay.

The announcement from Anza, the development team responsible for maintaining Agave, applies to both staked and unstaked nodes running the affected software. The developers also indicated that the network was continuing to operate normally.

The announcement follows a series of Solana validator software improvements introduced earlier this month, including further development of Agave and Firedancer.

An urgent software update does not necessarily mean that a blockchain is experiencing an outage. In Solana’s case, the more interesting question is how quickly its distributed network of operators can respond when developers identify a problem that cannot wait for a routine upgrade.

Anza directed operators to install version 4.4.2 of its validator software, telling them in its announcement:

The release is documented in Anza’s official GitHub repository, while compatible builds have also reportedly been made available by Jito-Solana and Harmonic.

Agave is one of the software implementations responsible for processing transactions and participating in Solana’s consensus mechanism. Validators running it help determine which transactions become part of the blockchain.

Unlike updating an application on a phone, updating validator software involves coordinating machines operated by independent organizations around the world. Developers can release a new version, but the operators themselves must deploy it.

Network monitoring data from Validator Info shows that both Agave 4.4.2 and Jito 4.4.2-jito have been released, while Firedancer’s latest listed version is 26.11.1. The availability of these releases does not, however, establish how many validators have installed them.

That makes the speed of adoption almost as interesting as the release itself.

A check of the Solana validator directory shows operators reporting different software versions, including Agave-derived implementations. However, a complete and independently verified breakdown of the latest upgrade’s adoption was not yet available.

The precise technical issue behind Anza’s urgent instruction remains to be fully established. Describing the release as a response to an exploit or an active network attack would therefore be premature.

The announcement comes just weeks after Solana introduced significant changes to its underlying infrastructure.

As NewsBTC previously reported, the Solana Foundation introduced protocol version 1.0 in November and moved away from describing the network as mainnet beta.

The distinction between the protocol version and the validator software version is important. Solana can establish a common set of network rules while individual software implementations continue to receive updates and fixes.

The network has also been pursuing faster transaction processing and shorter confirmation times through its Alpenglow consensus architecture.

Those improvements are valuable, but faster transactions are only useful if the infrastructure processing them remains dependable.

For ordinary users, Anza’s instruction is aimed at node operators rather than wallet holders. The announcement does not, by itself, establish a need for users to move their SOL or change how they interact with the network.

At the time of the dashboard snapshot, Solana had 655 active validators and five listed as delinquent. Approximately 423.44 million SOL was actively staked, representing 99.97% of the reported total stake. The figures offer a snapshot of network participation while operators are being asked to update their software, although they do not independently confirm the success of the upgrade.

The next meaningful development will be evidence that operators have installed the new release and that transaction processing remains stable throughout the rollout.

Solana has spent considerable time demonstrating how fast its network can become. This weekend’s upgrade offers another opportunity to assess something equally important: how well its infrastructure responds when speed is required outside of normal transaction processing.

#5025. 11-year Ethereum whale cashes out — What does it say about ETH’s price bottom?

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

Dormant sell-offs in a bear market can send two very different signals.

It may suggest that long-term holders have waning belief in an asset. Alternatively, it may just be an example of investors realizing profits having owned something for a long period of time. If the market interprets the sale as an indication that the market is nearing its bottom, FOMO might be in store.

Interestingly, a recent Ethereum whale’s move has brought this debate back into focus. The whale bought 100,000 ETH for just $31,000 in 2015. It has now sold its final 45,000 ETH for $75.3 million. In total, the investment generated over $87 million, translating to nearly 2,800x returns.

Naturally, the question is whether this was simply profit-taking.

Technically, Ethereum has fallen by 40%+ in 2026, bringing it down to currently around $1.7K. This is almost 65% less than the all-time high for ETH of $4.9K in 2025. This puts the whales’ last 45,000 ETH sell-off at an average of around $1,673, again similar to current prices, but well off cycle highs. Therefore, despite having enjoyed huge overall profits, the whale elected to sell in a deep market downturn, not in a rising market.

Could this be a whale securing profits, or is it a loss of confidence in Ethereum’s [ETH] recovery? With the price still deep below its cycle high, the dormant whale may have further motives behind the selling.

Usually, when dormant whales sell into market weakness, it raises the question of whether they see further downside that the broader market is yet to price in.

Technically, a 30% correction would also take ETH back towards its 2023 lows. A pivotal support area exists at $1.5K and should this be breached, further downside may follow. Especially given that bearishness has been on the rise. Indeed, the warning signs have been showing up in market data too.

Ethereum ETFs recorded $523.3 million in net outflows across eight trading sessions through 25th November. ETH has continued to underperform Bitcoin too. The broader altcoin market is also taking a hit. In fact, not a single one of the top-50 altcoins is up since Q4 began, while the median altcoin has lost 40% of its value in less than two months.

This points to weak capital inflows and limited risk appetite, making an Ethereum recovery harder to sustain.

Against this backdrop, the whale’s exit looks less like routine profit-taking and more like fading confidence in ETH’s recovery. This is important because whale selling near market bottoms can sometimes signal a buying opportunity. However, weak inflows and bearish market conditions make that case harder to support.

Thus, Ethereum’s weakness appears to be reaching even long-dormant wallets, adding further pressure to its bottoming thesis.

An 11-year-old Ethereum whale sold its final 45,000 ETH, raising questions about investor confidence.

Weak ETF inflows, falling altcoins, and ETH’s price decline put its recovery and $1.5K support at risk.

#5023. BlackRock Bitcoin ETF Loses $2.8 Billion in Eight Consecutive Trading Sessions

The BlackRock Bitcoin ETF has recorded nearly $2.8 billion in net withdrawals across eight consecutive trading sessions, accounting for approximately 81% of the capital leaving US spot Bitcoin ETFs over the period.

The latest figures from Farside Investors show that US spot Bitcoin ETFs registered $389 million in combined net outflows on Friday, November 27, extending a withdrawal streak that began on November 17.

BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) accounted for $327.2 million of Friday’s withdrawals.

Despite a shortened trading session following Thanksgiving, investors continued reducing their exposure through the largest Bitcoin ETF in the US.

Combined net withdrawals from US spot Bitcoin ETFs reached $3.44 billion over the eight trading sessions between November 17 and November 27.

Of that amount, approximately $2.79 billion came from BlackRock’s IBIT.

The fund recorded its heaviest withdrawals during this period on November 19 and 20, when investors redeemed a net $541.1 million and $544.7 million, respectively.

Net flows of US spot Bitcoin ETFs during the eight-session withdrawal streak. *Shortened post-Thanksgiving session; US markets were closed on November 26. Data: Farside Investors. Visualization: NewsBTC.

The concentration of withdrawals in IBIT is particularly important when interpreting aggregate Bitcoin ETF figures. Activity in a single fund has dominated the broader market’s recent net flows.

BlackRock’s size naturally makes it more likely to account for substantial movements of capital. Its share of the outflows, therefore, should not automatically be interpreted as evidence that investors are specifically losing confidence in BlackRock.

Friday’s $389 million in combined net outflows was lower than Wednesday’s $453 million, but the improvement was relatively modest.

BlackRock’s figures were particularly revealing. IBIT recorded $327.2 million in net withdrawals on Friday, barely below the $329.7 million recorded during Wednesday’s full trading session.

The shortened post-Thanksgiving trading window makes the comparison even less encouraging.

CoinGlass’s historical ETF flow data also illustrates how recent withdrawals contrast with the substantial inflows recorded during earlier stages of Bitcoin’s rally.

A smaller daily outflow does not necessarily signal that investors are returning. It may simply mean less capital left the funds during that particular session.

As NewsBTC previously reported, persistent withdrawals from spot Bitcoin ETFs have complicated the cryptocurrency’s attempts to establish a sustainable recovery.

It is important, however, to distinguish ETF redemptions from direct selling by BlackRock itself.

IBIT holds Bitcoin on behalf of its shareholders. Net withdrawals reflect activity within the fund’s creation and redemption mechanism, rather than necessarily representing a decision by BlackRock to sell Bitcoin from its own corporate balance sheet.

The figures also do not reveal whether the investors behind the redemptions are institutions, financial advisers or retail participants.

Monday’s trading session, the final US session of November, will offer another opportunity to assess whether demand for Bitcoin exposure is beginning to stabilize.

For now, Friday’s figures provide little evidence that the withdrawal pressure has materially eased. BlackRock’s fund experienced almost the same net outflows as Wednesday, despite a shorter trading session.

#5022. Americans are spending 2.1% more than in June but getting less than 1% more for their money

The latest household numbers provided some breathing room for consumers and little comfort for the Fed.

Americans had more income left over in October as their purchasing power improved and their spending barely changed.

The national saving rate recovered to 4.1%, close to its June level, giving households more room to absorb their expenses. Part of the income gain came from a one-time Medicare rebate, along with higher pay and dividend income, making the rebound slightly more reassuring than the summer numbers.

Through September, inflation-adjusted consumption was 0.92% above its June level, while after-tax income had gained just 0.18% in purchasing power. October's personal income report, released Nov. 25, brought those cumulative gains to 0.88% and 0.68%, respectively.

Spending grew slightly faster over the four months, though the gap between the two growth rates shrank to about 0.2%.

Cumulative percentage growth since June 2026. Both series remove inflation, and income is after personal taxes. Monthly BEA levels are seasonally adjusted annual rates, and gaps compare growth rates. Nov. 25 data vintage.

Source: BEA via FRED: real personal consumption expenditures · BEA via FRED: real disposable personal income

You can see the recovery on a smaller scale by applying the national saving rates to a hypothetical $5,000 in monthly after-tax income. June's 4.2% rate would leave $210, September's 3.6% would leave $180, and October's 4.1% would leave $205.

On that fixed income, October restored $25 of the $30 reduction in monthly saving capacity since June.

September spending is now estimated to have risen 0.6% in current dollars and 0.1% after removing inflation, compared with 0.5% and less than 0.1% in the original September report.

Real disposable income fell 0.2% that month instead of 0.3%, while the saving rate fell from 3.8% to 3.6%. The updated estimates put September's income slightly higher but left a smaller share available for saving.

But in October, disposable income rose 0.8% in current dollars, equivalent to a 0.5% gain in purchasing power, while consumer spending increased 0.3% in dollars. Inflation-adjusted consumption slipped by less than 0.1%, a decline small enough to round to 0%.

The monthly series for real disposable income and real consumer spending show most of the summer divergence between their growth rates disappearing in October.

Some of the extra income came from a one-time payment households will receive. Government social benefits increased partly because of the Medicare Improvement Fund premium rebate, which the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services described as a single $90 payment for 20.8 million eligible beneficiaries in Original Medicare Part B.

A $90 payment reaches a specified group of beneficiaries and enters national income through social benefits.

The rebate helped lift income, while its contribution to saving was not measured in the release.

The calculated program amount is not verified actual disbursement or a measured BEA contribution. Eligibility is limited to certain Original Medicare Part B beneficiaries. One-time totals and seasonally adjusted annualized income figures use different bases.

CMS announced $90 for 20.8 million eligible beneficiaries. Multiplication gives $1.872 billion, rounded to $1.87 billion, if all eligible receive the payment. BEA identifies its income-account treatment.

The calculated program amount is not verified actual disbursement or a measured BEA contribution. Eligibility is limited to certain Original Medicare Part B beneficiaries. One-time totals and seasonally adjusted annualized income figures use different bases.

Spending on gasoline and other energy goods fell by $2.1 billion annually, offsetting part of the increase elsewhere. Services supplied $52.1 billion of the $63.8 billion increase in total current-dollar consumption.

Please enable JavaScript to verify and send this form.

The BEA's spending breakdown attributes much of the services increase to nonprofit institutions and housing and utilities, with recreation and health care also contributing. These dollar amounts are seasonally adjusted annual rates, which express each month's pace of activity on a yearly scale.

Personal consumption expenditures (PCE) cover far more than what shoppers pay at a register. The bureau includes purchases made on people's behalf, such as medical care paid through an employer health plan.

The total combines fuel bought on the way to a doctor's office with the bill an insurer pays for the visit, so more dollars can pass through the accounts even when households receive little additional fuel or medical care.

Removing price increases helps distinguish those bigger bills from additional consumption. Between June and October, current-dollar spending rose 2.11%, while inflation-adjusted spending gained 0.88%.

Over the same period, the PCE price index increased 1.22%. In October alone, both the headline index and the core measure (which excludes food and energy) rose 0.3%, putting their annual increases at 3.8% and 3.3%.

For monetary policymakers, the report pairs stronger household purchasing power with almost no additional consumption in October, while inflation continues to run well above the Fed's 2% goal.

Higher real income gives consumers more room to keep buying in the months ahead. The flat consumption figure offers little evidence of an immediate acceleration in demand, although the price increases give officials reason to keep considering further rate increases.

At their October meeting, Fed officials described household spending as resilient, and a few participants discussed how higher prices for necessities were straining lower- and middle-income budgets, according to the meeting minutes.

Families able to postpone a purchase have more flexibility than workers who need a full tank to get to work, yet both contribute to the same national spending total.

The national accounts start with personal income, subtract current taxes, and then deduct personal outlays, which include consumption, interest payments, and certain transfers.

The amount left is personal saving, so October's 4.1% means $4.10 of every $100 in aggregate disposable income was left over. It gives no household-level account of who borrowed, sold an asset, or drew down a bank balance to keep paying their bills.

Personal saving as a percentage of disposable personal income. Seasonally adjusted monthly estimates, using the Nov. 25.

Source: BEA via FRED: personal saving rate

The Fed's 2% inflation objective uses the PCE price index, tying these same purchases directly to its rate deliberations. Officials held their policy rate at 3.75% to 4% in October, with two voters favoring a quarter-point increase.

Almost all participants judged that further increases would be appropriate if inflation and employment followed their expected paths, making that assessment conditional on the evidence still to arrive.

Investors weighing the size of a possible December rate increase have to distinguish the rebound in household income from the persistence of inflation.

Better purchasing power can support demand, while a one-time payment supplies less evidence of durable income growth than a recurring pay increase. For crypto borrowers, further increases in benchmark rates can raise interest bills on debt that resets with those rates, even when household finances look healthier.

The hypothetical $5,000 budget ended October with $205 available for saving, compared with $180 in September, a welcome recovery that brings it close to June's $210.

Actual households received different combinations of wages, benefits, and investment income, and the national figures can't tell us which families rebuilt their buffers.

For somebody using the $90 Medicare rebate to cover a bill, the benefit is immediate. Keeping that breathing room will require income that arrives as regularly as the bills do.

#5021. ‘Not your Silicon, not your keys’ — Ethereum’s Buterin calls for open-source chip design

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin has come up with an amendment to crypto’s oldest security motto, arguing that key safety increasingly depends on open-source chip designs.

In a blog post titled A shallow dive into open-source chip design, published on 26th November, Buterin shed light on the importance of making hardware designs publicly accessible and verifiable. He also argued that while the crypto industry has focused on securing software, cryptographic protocols, and private keys, underlying hardware remains an overlooked security risk.

Even if wallet software is secure, compromised hardware could expose sensitive information, including private keys and seed phrases.

Given the case in point, Buterin believes that verifying how a computer operates ultimately requires examining its underlying hardware, including transistors, silicon, and electrical circuits.

Even when software is open-source and independently audited, users have limited visibility into what the underlying chip actually does.

Probably the most frustrating thing about chip design is how opaque and proprietary the whole thing is.

To explain this risk better, he took reference from an attack involving a malicious implant with an eSIM inserted into a hardware wallet before it reaches consumers. Once activated, the implant can exfiltrate the wallet’s seed phrase.

Using this example, he also warned that attackers could replace legitimate chips with nearly identical versions containing additional malicious features. These, in turn, could bypass software-level security checks.

Not only this, but Buterin also believes that publicly accessible hardware designs would allow independent researchers to verify whether chips perform their intended functions.

However, publishing a chip’s Verilog code alone is insufficient. He argued that meaningful verification requires openness down to the GDS level, which describes the actual physical geometry of a chip’s components.

He also highlighted Process Design Kits (PDKs), which contain manufacturing-specific information and design rules needed to produce and validate chips.

Buterin highlighted IRIS, a chip-inspection technique being developed by hardware researcher Bunnie, which uses optical imaging to examine chip structures.

More sophisticated attacks involving changes to doping levels may require destructive methods such as Focused Ion Beam-Scanning Electron Microscopy (FIB-SEM).

He also proposed designing chips for easier inspection by enabling independent testing of smaller components, reducing dependence on fragile configurations, and making physical layouts more inspection-friendly.

Rather than expecting consumers to inspect chips themselves, he envisions professional auditors, journalists, and civil society groups using specialized equipment to verify manufacturers’ claims.

Finally, Buterin acknowledged that performance-intensive sectors such as AI are unlikely to adopt open-source manufacturing entirely. Instead, he is expecting a divide between performance-focused and security-focused hardware, with the latter prioritizing transparency and verifiability over efficiency.

He concluded it best by extending crypto’s familiar motto, “not your keys, not your coins”, with a hardware-focused warning.

#5020. Dogecoin Early History: Every Block Once Paid Up to 1 Million DOGE

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Dogecoin community member 'nformant' provides a throwback to Dogecoin's early days when miners could receive as much as 1 million DOGE for successfully producing a single block.

When Dogecoin launched on December 8, 2013, its original reward mechanism introduced randomness into mining payouts. Instead of receiving a fixed amount, miners earned a randomly determined reward. During the first 100,000 blocks, rewards could range up to 1 million DOGE. This meant that miners could receive substantially different payouts even when producing blocks under the same network conditions.

For Dogecoin's first 100 days, every Dogecoin block was a lottery ticket worth 2 to 1,000,000 DOGE, 'nformant' noted, citing the peculiar case of a miner who won 152,502 DOGE at block 2212 and claimed only 10,000 DOGE. The rest were never created, he added. 'nformant' provides a replay scenario for what might have transpired at block 2212, where the miner received a 152,502 DOGE reward and claimed only 10,000 DOGE.

For 100 days, every #Dogecoin block was a lottery ticket worth 2 to 1,000,000 DOGE. One miner won 152,502 and only claimed 10,000. The rest - never created. https://t.co/nJR0qenb6X The last draw ever: 384,843 DOGE in block 144,999! Block 2212 details: https://t.co/FCnPecP70n https://t.co/aZiIOWjVmh

This is drawn from the fact that from December 8, 2013, to March 17, 2014, every Dogecoin block paid a random reward between 2 and 1,000,000 DOGE. This changed to a maximum of 500,000 DOGE after block 100,000.

Dogecoin holders can get an idea of the miner rewards paid for each block up to 100,000 through a simulation called 'Dogecoin Lottery Replay' provided by 'nformant'. "The draw is computed from the previous block's hash, so anyone can re-compute it," with the input being the block number from 1 to 144,999.

"The last draw ever: 384,843 DOGE in block 144,999" indicates a total reward of 384,843 DOGE received at block 144,999.

The rewards for blocks 0–100,000 were randomized between 1 DOGE and 1,000,000 DOGE. The reward structure changed on February 14, 2014, at block 100,000, when the maximum random payout was reduced to 500,000 DOGE.

However, the randomized system did not last much longer. On March 17, 2014, beginning with block 145,000, Dogecoin switched to a fixed reward of 250,000 DOGE per block, ending the original random payout mechanism.

This continued until the 600,000th block, when the reward was fixed at 10,000 DOGE per block.

But in a bear market, the bigger question is: what are these traders actually betting on? Technically, SOL continues to slide, with its November losses now reaching 22%.

The key takeaway? SOL dropped as low as $64 this month, wiping out the gains from its Q2 rally, when it hit a local high of $125.

DEX volumes fell to $406 billion in Q4 from $667bn in Q3, according to DeFiLlama. Nonetheless, Solana continues to account for close to 23% of DEX volumes, highlighting that it still has moderately good trading volumes, despite the poor performance of its native token SOL.

Against this backdrop, the rise in Solana [SOL] long positions starts to make strategic sense.

High DEX trading volumes can drive significant transaction and space costs, which in turn can add further value to SOL. It can also increase revenue and offer market liquidity. T

raders may be betting that this sustained activity will eventually translate into stronger demand for SOL and support a price recovery.

Meanwhile, the SOL/BTC pair is also re-testing Q2 support, while BTC.D is nearing 60% resistance. Should it fail here, BTC.D may fall and funds may shift out of Bitcoin and into altcoins.

In doing so, Solana’s strong DEX data may prove fundamental. That said, the stakes couldn’t be higher.

Solana is heading for its worst year since inception.

Following a 20%+ correction in November, data from CoinGlass suggests that SOL looks set to end the month in negative territory. This would result in 9 out of 12 months being down for SOL in 2026. There were also 9 negative months for SOL in 2022. So, should December not reverse this trend, 2026 could even exceed this and prove to be Solana’s weakest year yet in terms of monthly performance.

Despite consistent month-on-month weakness, SOL’s annual ROI stands at -40%, slightly better than Ethereum’s -41%. It therefore appears that the issues facing Solana are not only those affecting the broader market but also relate specifically to the project.

Put simply, repeated monthly losses show how difficult it is for SOL bulls to hold support, leaving SOL susceptible to further downside.

According to AMBCrypto, this divergence could work against Solana.

The logic is simple: Strong DEX activity has yet to translate into buying pressure, while repeated monthly losses show that buyers are struggling to regain control. If this weakness continues, traders betting on a recovery could get caught on the wrong side. Leveraged liquidations could then add to selling pressure.

Thus, what looks like a recovery bet could quickly turn into a major bull trap.

Solana’s DEX activity remains strong, but its price continues to fall.

Rising long positions despite repeated monthly losses increase the risk of a bull trap and further liquidations.

The XRP token and NFT platform maintains that user assets remain safe, as user wallets and private keys were never accessed, and xrp cafe does not hold user wallets or private keys.

#5017. Bitcoin futures were just $38 above spot before Monday’s funding test

The New York Fed lent $23 billion on Black Friday. Monday’s repo usage and Tuesday’s overnight rate will give Bitcoin traders fresh funding benchmarks.

December Bitcoin futures were just $38 above Coinbase spot at Friday’s early settlement, before borrowing and trading costs. Separately, the New York Fed lent $23 billion in overnight repurchase agreements on Black Friday, up from zero on Wednesday, Nov. 25. The loans come due Monday, when a batch of Treasury securities is due to settle.

The New York Fed’s repo results show that the morning operation accepted $22.75 billion against Treasury collateral and $400 million against agency mortgage-backed securities at a 4% offering rate. Counterparties requested no funds that afternoon. The overnight loans span three calendar days across the weekend.

The Treasury auction calendar lists 2-, 5- and 7-year notes, a 20-year bond and a reopened 10-year inflation-protected note for Nov. 30 settlement. Buyers pay for new securities while holders of maturing debt receive cash. The net effect on available cash depends on maturities, other Treasury cash flows and how dealers finance the securities.

CME’s preliminary Friday bulletin marked December Bitcoin futures at $59,885. Coinbase’s one-minute candle closed at $59,847 in the minute ending at 1 p.m. ET, the cutoff for CME’s early holiday settlement. Using unrounded prices, the $37.90 gap worked out to about 0.86% annualized over 27 calendar days before the contract’s Dec. 24 expiry.

A cash-and-carry trader buys Bitcoin and sells futures, aiming to earn that price difference as the two legs converge. Friday’s comparison uses a futures settlement and the last spot trade on a single exchange in the preceding minute. Actual returns depend on prices a trader can execute, the cost of borrowing and the cash needed to meet futures margin.

That 0.86% gross annualized premium sat below the latest published Secured Overnight Financing Rate, or SOFR, of 3.95% for Wednesday. The rate tracks overnight loans backed by Treasuries. A Bitcoin desk’s credit and collateral terms can differ, and the overnight reading covers a much shorter period than the futures trade.

29th October’s Binance hack is still in the news, making waves today thanks to North Korean hackers who are now attempting to launder stolen cryptos.

Rather than immediately converting the stolen assets into cash, the hackers are moving them through different cryptocurrency services to make their transactions harder to trace.

According to blockchain analytics firms Chainalysis and Elliptic, stolen cryptos worth more than $600 million have already passed through THORChain. Another $342 million have reportedly moved through a CoinJoin service.

Since THORChain does not require Know Your Customer (KYC) checks or censor transactions, it does not require users to verify their identities before making swaps. This has made the protocol useful for hackers attempting to move the stolen Binance funds.

THORChain is Financial Freedom The Cypherpunk Way.

The FBI has already identified wallet addresses associated with the attackers. It recently urged crypto service providers, including THORChain’s network operators, to block transactions linked to them.

And yet, despite this warning, the protocol has continued to process transactions associated with the laundering operation. In fact, THORChain has generated up to $1 million in fees from these swaps as per TRM Labs estimates.

Additionally, hackers have also used CoinJoin, a transaction-mixing technique designed to conceal transaction trails.

Well, to cash out, the hackers will still need to transfer the cryptocurrency through additional services. These would potentially include over-the-counter (OTC) brokers, where digital assets can be exchanged for traditional currencies or other forms of value.

In the words of Ari Redbord, Global Head of Policy at U.S blockchain analysis company TRM Labs,

They don’t have to get a lot ​off in order to make this all worthwhile for them.

These additional transactions create further opportunities for investigators and law enforcement agencies to identify and freeze the funds.

Around $2.85 billion has already been frozen by token issuers. However, the remaining assets are still in circulation, raising concerns. Also, TRM Labs has estimated that the laundering operation could continue for months or even years.

This update comes on the heels of the United States’ DOJ filing a forfeiture action to recover more than $1.1 billion in cryptocurrencies stolen in the hack.

#5011. What a 12-cent Bitcoin ETF option reveals about crash protection

A March put pays at expiry only if IBIT falls below $10. The same premium can fit several outcomes, including losses unrelated to Bitcoin’s signatures.

A put option on BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF (IBIT) that gives the buyer the right to sell shares for $10 apiece through March 19, 2027, last traded at 12 cents per share in Optionistics’ Nov. 27 data.

With the shares at $33.86, it would take a 70.5% decline just to reach the strike.

The payout depends on the ETF share price, while the premium leaves open how likely AI is to undermine the signatures that authorize Bitcoin transactions.

Optionistics shows a 12-cent ask and last trade on Nov. 27. ChartExchange’s history for the same contract shows a trade at $0.06 on Oct. 15 and an opening trade at $0.12 on Nov. 17.

If shares of BlackRock’s Bitcoin ETF finish at $2 on expiration day, the right to sell at $10 is worth $8 a share, or $800 for one standard contract.

Before fees, the expiration break-even is $9.88. At $10 or above, exercising at expiration has no value, and the buyer loses the premium if still holding the put.

The Options Clearing Corporation’s ETF specifications allow exercise before expiration too, so these figures describe the economics at expiry under standard settlement.

Suppose the premium is $0.12 and the ETF has only two possible prices at expiration: zero or $10 and above. The put pays $10 per share at zero and nothing at $10 or above. Dividing the premium by the only positive payoff gives a 1.2% pricing weight for the zero-price outcome.

If the one-paying outcome is $2 per share and the payoff drops to $8 per share, the same $0.12 premium now fits a 1.5% weight. If the one-paying outcome is $9, the payoff is $1, and the weight is 12%.

The $10 IBIT put has a larger payoff when the ETF finishes further below its strike. A two-outcome illustration shows why the same premium fits different pricing weights.

Illustration. IBIT at $0 gives a $10 payoff per share. The other outcome is $10 or higher and pays zero.

Illustration. IBIT at $2 gives a $8 payoff per share. The other outcome is $10 or higher and pays zero.

Illustration. IBIT at $9 gives a $1 payoff per share. The other outcome is $10 or higher and pays zero.

The 12-cent premium can fit very different pricing weights when the assumed payoff changes.

Hypothetical illustrations exclude early exercise, interest and fees and assume standard settlement. The displayed weights belong to separate models. They do not estimate the odds of a cryptography break.

At expiration, subtract the IBIT share price from the $10 strike, with a floor of zero. For each illustrative case, divide the observed $0.12 ask by that case’s payoff per share and convert to a percent. Each case assumes its selected share price is the only paying outcome. Standard contracts cover 100 shares.

Hypothetical illustrations exclude early exercise, interest and fees and assume standard settlement. The displayed weights belong to separate models. They do not estimate the odds of a cryptography break.

Researchers at the New York Fed and the Bank of England have used prices across strikes to estimate distributions of future asset prices. The resulting risk-neutral weights describe how the market prices those outcomes under a model.

Please enable JavaScript to verify and send this form.

Identifying a cause requires evidence beyond the distribution of IBIT prices. A prolonged sell-off or a custody shock could send the fund below the strike, while a signature break could prompt a steep sell-off that still leaves shares above it.

A fixed $10 strike moves closer as the ETF falls, even if traders’ assessment of why it might fall stays the same.

A Bitcoin signature proves control of the private key needed to spend. The concern is that a new algorithm could make it practical to recover that private key from its public counterpart and spend without the owner’s consent.

On Nov. 27, the Cryptology ePrint Archive listed a preprint from Zhejiang University researchers Shuchang Liu, Bingsheng Zhang and Kui Ren.

The authors claim a new theoretical, subexponential running-time bound for solving discrete logarithms on prime-order elliptic curves, conditional on an earlier OpenAI construction.

Adam Back pointed to memory demands as a practical constraint for 256-bit curves, which is a separate test from improving a theoretical running-time bound.

Chamath Palihapitiya’s Nov. 27 essay made a broader argument that AI could shorten the time it takes to find better algorithms. He distinguished Bitcoin’s elliptic-curve signatures from RSA, which relies on the practical difficulty of factoring large numbers.

Ledger CTO Charles Guillemet identified separate rumors about factoring, elliptic curves and the quantum resistance of Ring-LWE. Meanwhile, computer scientist Scott Aaronson said he knew of forthcoming theoretical work that posed no imminent danger to deployed systems.

On Nov. 10, Glassnode reported that about 7 million BTC, or 35.4% of the supply, had a visible public key.

Some Bitcoin outputs reveal the key by design, while others hide it on-chain behind a hash until it is revealed through spending. If researchers found a practical way to recover private keys from public ones, coins in the already-visible group would face the most immediate risk from that method.

Bitcoin developers have proposed ways to reduce that exposure.

Draft BIP 360 proposes an output type that limits long-duration exposure by removing the Taproot key path and its visible output key, while draft BIP 361 outlines a migration away from legacy signatures after a post-quantum output type becomes available.

The Ethereum Foundation said on Nov. 23 it had doubled its protocol security team and was pursuing hash-based alternatives, while researcher Justin Drake proposed a December 2028 transition target.

The next useful data for options traders would be sustained changes in the cost of protection across strikes and expiries, measured alongside changes in the ETF’s price.

Meanwhile, the more consequential evidence for protocol developers would be an independently confirmed algorithm with measured resource requirements on real-world cryptographic parameters, or a concrete step toward migration.

In a significant development for the XRP Ledger, two key amendments, Lending Protocol and Single Asset Vault, have entered their two-week activation window.

LendingProtocolV1_1 has been up for voting since September 29, 2026; it was introduced in XRPL version 3.4.0, although the initial lending protocol amendment has been up for voting since February 2, 2026.

LendingProtocolV1_1 extends the LendingProtocol and SingleAssetVault amendments with a new closed-ended vault and cash-basis accounting. At press time, it has secured 88.24% support, well above the required 80% threshold, with 30 out of 34 validators voting in favor. The earliest possible activation date is Dec 11, 2026, at 2:22 PM UTC, as validator support for the amendment must stay above 80% the throughout. If it slips to 80% or lower even once, the amendment is rejected and the 14-day timer starts over.

The Lending Protocol (XLS 66) enables on-chain, fixed-term, uncollateralized loans using pooled funds from a Single Asset Vault. The initial lending protocol amendment targets a mainnet activation date of December 11, 2026, as well.

In a similar development, the Single Asset Vault amendment, which has been up for voting since February 2, 2026, has surpassed the required 80% threshold, gaining 88.24% validator support as 30 out of 34 validators voted in favor.

Single Asset Vault creates a structure for aggregating assets from multiple depositors and is intended to be used with the on-chain Lending Protocol. This feature activation is expected no earlier than Dec 9, 2026, at 7:38 PM UTC, if the required 80% validator support holds all the way.

As lending is coming to the XRPL, XRP Ledger Foundation Director of Community Hussein Zangana (Vet) says this could be huge for XRP and issued assets, highlighting the potential for greater capital efficiency and asset mobility across the network.

Lending is coming to the XRP Ledger and it's huge for XRP and issued assets. XRPL Era of collateral, yield farming, mobility and capital efficiency. - XRP and issued assets for collateral. - No smart contract risk, it's baked into the XRPL. - Ready for institutional credit with Permissioned Vault (for KYC/AML etc) - Yield bearing tokens! When you deposit into a vault, you get a yield bearing liquid token back (LP). - Which enables leverage of multiple vaults via LP tokens, take one vault's liquid tokens and put it elsewhere as collateral! - Building block for treasury and asset management, putting their XRP and assets to work. 24/7 enabling collateral mobility. All votes for the amendments have a healthy buffer of 30 votes as well thanks to other validators!

Users will be able to deposit XRP and other issued assets into vaults as collateral. In return, depositors receive liquid, yield-bearing tokens representing their positions. The lending functionality is baked into the XRP Ledger, which reduces smart contract-related risks.

Vet also highlighted the potential of Permissioned Vaults, which could support institutional lending requirements, including Know Your Customer (KYC) and Anti-Money Laundering (AML) compliance.

The features could also provide new opportunities for corporate treasury and asset management. Institutions holding XRP and issued assets may eventually be able to put those holdings to work through collateralized lending and yield-generating strategies.

#5005. The Fed’s Sunday payments plan reveals why 24/7 finance needs more than faster technology

Banks preparing for Sunday payments have a familiar request for the Fed: keep the lending window open, too.

Suppose a customer asks a bank on a Sunday to wire $100 million and has the money in the account. The bank's treasurer has a second balance to check, because the bank settles the payment by moving money out of its own account at the Fed and into the receiving bank's account there.

Banks use these accounts to pay one another, and the dollars they hold in them are called reserves. Say the sending bank holds $80 million in reserves and the Federal Reserve allows it to overdraw during the day.

It can send the full $100 million, leaving its Fed account $20 million below zero, then wait for an incoming payment to cover the difference.

On an ordinary weekday, a treasurer whose incoming wire runs late has several places to look for a short-term loan. On a Sunday, under a plan the Fed expects to introduce in 2028 or 2029, the wire service is scheduled to close at 7 p.m. Eastern, and the bank will need to have covered its overdraft by then.

The customer has the money, while the sending bank uses its own Fed balance to settle the payment.

The bank needs an incoming payment or borrowing to cover its overdraft by the scheduled Sunday close.

Illustration assumes eligibility for intraday credit and ignores other transactions. The receiving account amount is an increase, not its total balance. Sunday service is planned for 2028 or 2029. Discount window expansion is undecided.

Hypothetical balances from the article: $80 million minus a $100 million wire equals a $20 million overdraft. A $20 million inflow restores zero. Operating rules and policy status are from the Fed.

Illustration assumes eligibility for intraday credit and ignores other transactions. The receiving account amount is an increase, not its total balance. Sunday service is planned for 2028 or 2029. Discount window expansion is undecided.

On a survey released Nov. 20, 41 of 91 institutions said access to the Fed's discount window would be important during at least some of the extra operating hours.

Please enable JavaScript to verify and send this form.

Eligible banks can use the window to pledge assets as collateral and borrow from their regional Federal Reserve Bank, giving them another source of cash when other funding falls through. Twenty-nine respondents wanted the same borrowing hours they get on a weekday.

With a Sunday closing time already set, banks are waiting to see whether the Fed will also make loans as that hour approaches.

Fedwire, the Fed's system for moving large payments between banks, already opens on Sunday night. The wrinkle is that the existing 9 p.m. opening belongs to Monday's business day.

Under the new schedule, it will also open at 9 p.m. Eastern on Saturday, giving banks a 22-hour Sunday business day before it closes at seven and reopens two hours later for Monday.

Customer wires have an earlier Fedwire cutoff of 6:45 p.m. Eastern, and banks can set their own earlier deadlines. The long weekly break, from Friday at 7 p.m. to Saturday at 9 p.m., stays in place.

Banks can choose whether to work the additional days, which include weekday holidays. The Fed will also extend the hours of the National Settlement Service, through which private payment arrangements settle what their members owe one another.

Its day ends half an hour before Fedwire's, and the latest implementation update still puts both services' expansion in 2028 or 2029.

The Fed's operating rules allow money to be deposited at a bank that's closed. The Fed credits the receiving bank's account when the wire comes through, but if Sunday falls outside that bank's own funds-transfer business day, the bank can wait until its next one to act on the order.

Payment between the banks can be final on Sunday while the person expecting the money has to wait to use it.

For the treasurer waiting for the $20 million, the same patchwork of working hours makes borrowing much more complicated. Dollars held elsewhere in the banking system help only if their owner is available and willing to lend.

During the public consultation, the payments operator The Clearing House asked for a way to identify which counterparties would be operating. Trading firms offering weekend access to US markets face a similar calculation when deciding how much business they can finance while their usual counterparties have the weekend off.

One way to ensure the bank has its $20 million on Sunday is to put an extra $20 million in its Fed account on Friday.

Of the 91 institutions surveyed, 22 expected to hold temporarily larger reserve balances for weekends and holidays, 31 saw no need, and 38 were unsure.

Together, the respondents held roughly 75% of all reserves in the banking system, although each institution counted equally and the survey sought no dollar estimate for those extra balances.

September 2026 Senior Financial Officer Survey, released Nov. 20, on the importance of discount window access on Sundays and weekday holidays. The first two categories total 41 institutions.

Source: Federal Reserve, September 2026 SFOS, question 15

Another option is to borrow reserves through the federal funds market, where loans are generally unsecured and run overnight. Only eight respondents expected to be ready to trade federal funds on the additional operating days, and being ready to trade leaves open which side of the transaction they'll take.

In a separate part of the survey, 41 institutions said they were active borrowers in that market and just five said they were active lenders.

The New York Fed identifies the Federal Home Loan Banks as the country's principal federal funds lenders. The bank survey establishes no commitment from those lenders to operate on the extra days, so its eight prospective trading desks offer only a partial view of the market that might emerge.

That uncertainty gives the discount window some appeal, especially among domestic banks. Of the 56 domestic respondents, 35 valued at least some extra-day access, compared with six of 35 foreign respondents.

Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan argued for opening the window on weekends and holidays, a decision that belongs to the Fed's Board of Governors. Even if the Board agrees, banks planning to borrow against Treasury securities may have work to do on Friday.

Fedwire Securities, which they use to move those assets into position, will keep its existing hours, requiring banks to arrange that collateral before the weekend.

The Fed expects relatively little money to move during the additional hours at first, and banks can begin with limited operations.

Stablecoin businesses already deal with similar availability differences. The bank redemption channel DBS and Circle announced is for eligible institutions, while dollar payouts from Invesco's tokenized reserve fund follow the fund's own business-day rules.

If the $20 million arrives as expected, the treasurer goes home, and the customer who sent $100 million never hears about the overdraft, which is how uneventful a Sunday wire ought to be. The treasurer would simply like the number of somebody who'll pick up the phone at a quarter to seven.

#4997. Bitcoin Has Become Boring, Finally

Bitcoin isn't a shiny new technology any more, it is established, and it is here to stay.

The 2019 Lightning conference in Berlin was lit: five hundred “cypherpunks” getting each other high on visions of a future with peer-to-peer electronic cash. Attending a bitcoin conference back in the day felt like being a teenager at a friend’s party while their parents were out of town. It was exciting and new. The feeling was the opposite of FOMO: something big was happening, we were on the inside, and the rest of the world was going to envy us. It was the kind of party that you could only have when the adults weren’t looking. Whenever someone bought a beer (with bitcoin), everyone would hoot and holler and record it on their phones for Instagram/Twitter (it was still called Twitter).

Lightning was the bleeding edge. We called it “the Lightning Network” (capitalized, if you please), and talking about it felt like talking about string theory: something so far out you’re not even sure it’s real. I spent a lot of time invoking the abacus.

Those are the times some of us remember fondly and keep trying to relive at bitcoin conferences today. That’s why we engage in rituals like drone shows, Satoshi Rockamoto sets, beefsteak dinners, and video game tournaments for sats, but it’s not the same. The ratio of bitcoin OG speakers to suits is shifting. Many event rooms are half empty, and the halls and meeting rooms are full of people negotiating cap tables and profit-sharing splits.

The adults haven’t shut the party down, but they have crashed it, and it kinda feels like their party now. The most exciting thing I noticed at the last bitcoin conference I attended was that nothing exciting happened.

The road to boring is seldom smooth. Technological innovation benefits from passion and bold ideas. People work harder on a project when they feel strongly about it and identify closely with like-minded collaborators. That’s where tech subcultures, their rituals, and their dogmas come from. But such passion and tribalism feed conflict, at least for a while until the tech goes mainstream, and normies, who couldn’t care less about subculture squabbles, take over.

This progression from an exciting new technology that inspires strong emotions to a humdrum utility is not unusual. World-changing innovations often (always?) start with a committed subculture that identifies fiercely with their weird tech before the mainstream adopts it and soon expects it. In fact, this trajectory has become the standard doctrine of tech marketing. For example, in the early days of the internet, early adopters wrote a Declaration of the Independence of Cyberspace, picking a fight with states and corporations despite having nothing to back it up but chatrooms and dreams.

One case that resembles the early days of bitcoin was the war of the currents between high-voltage AC current and low-voltage DC current in the 1880s-1890s. Both featured big personalities stunning audiences with flashy demos at conferences. Edison and Westinghouse wowed crowds with their lightbulbs that made artificial light, just like bitcoiners in 2019 wowed YouTube by buying beer with bitcoin. And both cases featured rabid subcultures that accused each other of putting the future of the technology, if not of humanity, at stake. In the 1880s, the issue was whether AC was more deadly to humans and animals than DC; in the 2010s it was whether limiting the size of bitcoin’s blocks to 1MB would perpetuate monetary servitude forever.

In both cases, there were devoted subcultures whose disagreements helped the technology to mature before the tech crossed the chasm of exoticism to become the new, boring normal. Both are now largely managed by experts on pragmatic principles, not passionate conviction. Conferences went from spectacular showcases for technological miracles to sedate affairs where professionals debate and agree on industry standards. Pragmatism and consensus replaced ideology and dissent. In both instances things got boring, and boring was actually better.

Bitcoin is getting boring, although what that means and how it’s come to be that way depends on your point of view. As always, where you stand depends on where you sit.

Generally speaking, there are two broad points of view on what bitcoin is and is for. And though they started in different places, they’re both coming to a common conclusion: bitcoin is more boring than ever. So let’s review these two points of view, how they view bitcoin now, and why both would agree that the status quo is now so awfully, wonderfully boring.

The basic existential question that defined bitcoin’s first decade is settled: bitcoin is not a scam, and it’s not going away. That status is stable largely because bitcoin is now too big to fail, with a market cap exceeding a trillion dollars.

Much of this scale is thanks to the millions of people who want to own bitcoin as part of their savings, but not necessarily to trade and circulate it. In other words, they see bitcoin as a better form of gold, not cash. These savers want to integrate bitcoin into their fiat portfolio, just like any other asset. They aren’t terribly concerned about bitcoin’s status as a medium of exchange so long as it becomes firmly established as a viable, tradable commodity.

People investing in bitcoin are happy when the number goes up, and it generally does (you might have to zoom out on the price graph a bit, depending on the week). Bitcoin used to be a rollercoaster; now it’s more of a hike. The ups and downs still happen, but they’re gentler and a bit more predictable. How boring.

Bitcoin’s price started to settle down as mainstream finance started growing more comfortable with it as an asset. Whereas conventional finance used to want governments to shut bitcoin down, there is now about $100B worth of bitcoin held in ETFs and traded on ordinary equity markets. Major banks used to shun bitcoin, and now they accept it as collateral. Bitcoin is a regular feature in corporate treasuries, and some companies exist just to hold bitcoin. Strategy is worth about $55B on the open market, and it holds about $63B worth of bitcoin, so the entire company is a discounted bitcoin wallet. Bitcoin is also a regular feature in retirement accounts, pension allocations, and sovereign wealth funds. Thinking of bitcoin as another kind of asset ripe for institutional and retail investors now makes a lot of sense, because that’s what it is.

Why are these canny investors bored? It seems that all the exciting developments leading to bitcoin becoming a valuable asset have already happened. If the goal was integration into the world of conventional finance, it has incontrovertibly been achieved. You can’t YOLO on bitcoin any more than you can YOLO on gold. The milestones are all in the history section of the Wikipedia page, not on the roadmap.

People who wanted bitcoin to become a tradable asset are bored because mainstream finance has effectively tamed bitcoin. It is easily tradable, and its trading volumes are remarkable. It is digital gold, just with a slightly steeper curve and a little more volatility, which is exactly what these folks always wanted.

The main alternative to seeing bitcoin as a mainstream investment asset is to view it as monetary dynamite to ignite a revolution. People subscribing to this point of view wanted bitcoin to blossom into a system of peer-to-peer electronic cash that would first operate in parallel to the mainstream monetary system before supplanting it. These radicals wanted to see the banks collapse, not accept bitcoin as collateral. It was monetary insurrection, not incremental change.

This radical point of view is still around, but the wind has gone out of its combative sails for a few reasons.

First, there has been a generational shift. Many of the people who were pushing the revolutionary vision of bitcoin in their 20s fifteen years ago have moved on. Some got rich and retired or started to see and use bitcoin more as a tradable asset. For others, bitcoin never achieved the success they dreamt of, but it was successful enough that fighting for its future no longer felt necessary.

Second, AI is the new cool kid on the tech block. Instead of building vending machines for beer that accept bitcoin, enthusiasts who want to hack the system are now decompiling games with AI. No VC will waste a second on a pitch deck that doesn’t have AI on at least half of the slides. Miners are turning their server stacks and power contracts into AI data centers. Curious engineers have a new, much bigger toy to play with.

Third, mainstream bitcoin fans on Wall Street simply consume too much bandwidth. Not surprisingly, banks, publicly traded companies, and financial institutions with billions in their pockets are dominating panels at conferences and supplying the talking heads for financial news shows. They want to discuss topics like volatility and discount rates instead of personal sovereignty and individual financial freedom. Fighting against the system is not a narrative they can sell while representing the interests of that very system.

Fourth, bitcoin usage has moved past the radical mantras and progressed in a different direction. The dream of bitcoin becoming the standard payment medium in a circular economy where everyone buys coffee with bitcoin (why is it always coffee?) is starting to feel like an alternative history in a parallel universe.

A circular economy is simply not the role in society bitcoin has grown into. Instead of everyday payments, bitcoin is the medium of global value transfer. It has evolved into a technology to move real money across borders as remittances, into a settlement layer between various crypto assets, and into a store of value that people constantly buy, sell, and trade. It’s become a valuable network of rails that even stablecoins are happy to use.

Fixating on coffee purchases obscures the remarkable scale bitcoin has achieved. Somewhere between $1.6 and $4.1 trillion was settled on-chain between Q1 and Q3 2026 (depending on how you count). PayPal processed $1.79 trillion in all of 2025. The average payment on PayPal is about $70. The average bitcoin transaction (using the strict counting method) is $10,000. With bitcoin moving trillions in value, we can stop worrying about coffee.

Bitcoin may not have cornered retail payments, but it’s a mature and highly liquid asset. It’s an industry unto itself. It has found its place in the economy, and it’s thriving. Despite the lack of revolutionary fireworks, bitcoin is changing mainstream finance by opening new possibilities and financially enfranchising new user groups. That’s still worth celebrating.

You know what’s really boring? Electricity infrastructure. You know what no one can live without despite how boring it is? Electricity infrastructure.

When revolutionary technologies fade into the background of everyday life, when people use them constantly without thinking about them, they become boring, and they become essential. Buying a beer with Lightning is no longer exciting because we can now expect that it will just work without fanfare. Being able to say “it will just work” sounds boring, but it’s a clear sign of triumph.

Bitcoiners and builders need to adjust to this beautiful, boring reality. We can stop annoying our neighbors with orange pills. It’s about utility, not evangelism. Utility means building rails that bitcoin and stablecoins can use together seamlessly, adding bitcoin to mainstream fintech apps, and building new financial applications on top of the bitcoin chain. Perhaps none of this will light the fireworks at the radicals’ victory party or replace T-bills as the base layer of global finance, but every user who discovers the unique utility of bitcoin is further evidence of its mainstream adoption.

What we have is a thriving technology that enables us to do miraculous new things, and it’s achieved an undeniable scale, such that it is now too big to fail. That’s fantastic. It may not be the future we were dreaming about seven years ago in Berlin, but it’s wonderful in its own right, and it’s worth cultivating and celebrating.

Even though nobody sets out to grow up and become boring one day, it’s still a valid kind of success. It means you’ve made it, and you’re doing fine. Boring is what happens when things just work and things have just worked out. So we didn’t break the world with bitcoin. Oh well. We’re making a new one. A party with adults present is still a party. And maybe we’re now the adults. So dance while you wait for the dollar to collapse 😉

#4995. AI could prove P = NP and still fail to crack a single Bitcoin key

A qualifying lab announcement could settle the market, and Bitcoin holders would still need to see how quickly someone can sign for a full-size key.

The latest fad on social media appears to be claiming that cryptography has been secretly broken by AI labs. The result has been an avalanche of “newly qualified mathematicians” claiming that an announcement that P = NP is coming and Bitcoin is doomed.

Both of those takes do well on social feeds, but how well do they hold up to the actual math?

Firstly, and probably most importantly, even if someone proved P = NP, the fastest known way to break a particular cryptographic scheme could still take millions of years on real hardware. A proof would guarantee that polynomial-time algorithms exist for certain problems underlying cryptography. The proof itself might give us no usable algorithm, and an algorithm it did yield could still be impractically slow.

The phrase “as easy to solve as to check” is where the confusion likely comes in. It means both tasks can be done in polynomial time. The two polynomials can be wildly different. Imagine checking an answer takes n^2 steps and finding it takes n^10. At n=256 and a billion steps a second, checking takes about 66 microseconds and finding takes about 38 million years.

P vs NP is about how the amount of work grows as inputs get larger. So, would proving the reverse (that P ≠ NP) indicate Bitcoin is even more secure? Yes and no.

First, for anyone wondering, it wouldn't prove Bitcoin is quantum-resistant. That result would concern classical computation. Shor’s quantum algorithm for discrete logarithms already exists independently of P vs NP. Its practical relevance to Bitcoin depends on whether a quantum computer can run it at the scale required for Bitcoin’s signatures.

However, it would prove that some problems have solutions a classical computer can check quickly, even though no classical algorithm can solve every instance in polynomial time. That would still leave open the question that matters to Bitcoin holders: how hard is it to recover the private key behind a typical Bitcoin public key?

What's getting a lot of people worried is how high the odds of P vs NP being solved by AI this year are getting. However, as usual with these sorts of things, there's a lot of nuance missing.

An AI lab could announce it had proved that P equals NP. It could also announce it had proved that P does not equal NP. Either announcement could pay $1 per Yes share on Polymarket’s year-end math bet. For a Bitcoin holder, the practical question would be whether anyone could produce a valid signature for a full-size key without the owner’s secret.

Polymarket displayed 13% for Yes at 20:29 GMT on Nov. 27. CryptoSlate’s snapshot recorded a 12.5¢ bid and a 12.6¢ ask. The midpoint fell from 12.55¢ in that snapshot to 7.05¢ in the Nov. 28 check. The market displayed 7% on Nov. 28, with a 7.0¢ bid and 7.1¢ ask in the 10:01 GMT market data.

To qualify under Polymarket’s rules, an eligible AI lab or its official representative has to announce a complete solution by 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 31, 2026, or 4:59 a.m. GMT on Jan. 1, 2027. The lab has to present it as work by the lab, its researchers or its models. Joint work can count. A congratulatory post about an outside researcher falls short even if that researcher used the lab’s model.

The rules waive further confirmation from Clay or any other organization. They leave the direction of the proof open, and the outcome and event clarification feeds were empty when checked on Nov. 28. Either direction appears to fit on CryptoSlate’s reading. The contract prices the chance of a qualifying announcement. It offers no separate odds for equality, a practical break of Bitcoin signatures or a mining advantage.

A neighboring bet shows why the announcement matters. Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge released a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis on Nov. 20 and credited Claude. On Nov. 21, the Lean FRO and Mathlib Initiative said independent checks had verified both the precise theorem statement and its proof in their joint statement.

Six days after that statement, the separate Riemann contract was still accepting orders at 20:29 GMT on Nov. 27, according to CryptoSlate’s venue snapshot. The record establishes that orders were open and leaves the reason for the timing unresolved. The proof check established what Alpöge had shown. The market rules also make the identity of the claimant part of the settlement test.

Stephen Cook’s description of the problem for the Clay Mathematics Institute starts with yes-or-no questions. P covers problems a deterministic classical algorithm can solve in polynomial time. NP covers problems for which the computer can check a proof of a Yes answer in polynomial time, provided the proof is short enough relative to the input. The question is whether a fast way to check a candidate always implies a fast way to solve the problem, in that mathematical sense. The recent VP versus VNP result concerns algebraic circuits.

If P = NP, that result would also put the associated search problems in polynomial time. Scott Aaronson explains why this would rule out one-way functions in their standard theoretical sense. These are functions designed to be easy to compute and hard to reverse. The word polynomial describes an upper bound on how the work grows with input length. An algorithm can satisfy that definition and still take longer than a lifetime at Bitcoin’s actual key size. A proof might also leave researchers without a usable implementation. Scott Aaronson’s P versus NP survey

If P ≠ NP, some efficiently checkable problems would have no deterministic classical polynomial-time algorithm that works on every input. The finding would leave the hardness of a typical Bitcoin key and the cost of finding a valid block open.

Peter Shor’s quantum discrete-logarithm algorithm would still apply. In a more recent study, Ryan Babbush and his co-authors modeled a 256-bit elliptic-curve discrete-logarithm computation in minutes with fewer than 500,000 physical qubits, assuming planar superconducting hardware and a 0.1% physical error rate. Those figures describe what their proposed machine could do under the model.

Bitcoin nodes can check a signature quickly. To find out what a claimed breakthrough means at the deployed key size, look for independent reproduction on a fresh challenge and a full-size test key, with the secret and its signer kept out of reach. Reproducible recovery of the secret would also count. A useful report would name the signature scheme and hardware, give the elapsed time and memory use, and show how often the test worked across independently generated keys. Bitcoin’s traditional ECDSA and Taproot’s Schnorr signatures use the same curve, secp256k1.

A Taproot payment puts the public output key in the transaction that creates it. A capability that depends on a public key could matter for the entire time that payment sits unspent.

A fresh pay-to-witness-public-key-hash payment, or P2WPKH, initially shows a hash. If the key has never appeared elsewhere, it normally becomes public when the owner broadcasts the spend. A capability could be fast enough to matter for a Taproot payment that has sat untouched for days and too slow to matter during that newly disclosed key’s window. Disclosure can also leave other unspent payments to the same reused key exposed after the revealing spend confirms.

A capability that needs a visible public key would face different exposure windows for the two payments.

This diagram assumes a fresh P2WPKH key. Reuse can leave other unspent payments tied to a key that is already public.

Bitcoin targets an average block interval of ten minutes. A block header carries a timestamp set by its miner. In CryptoSlate’s analysis of 135 consecutive block-header timestamp differences for Nov. 26 UTC, the median was 7 minutes 56 seconds. Sixteen gaps exceeded 20 minutes. Three child blocks had a timestamp earlier than their parent’s. The calculation takes the differences in block height order and keeps the negative values. The first gap uses a parent block with a Nov. 25 timestamp.

An earlier child timestamp is possible because Bitcoin requires it to exceed the median of the previous 11 blocks. The sample describes the timestamps miners put in their headers. To measure the time available around a specific spend, an observer would need to record when they first received the transaction and when they first saw a block confirm it.

Counts for 135 consecutive differences on Nov. 26, 2026 UTC, including the first block’s previous-day parent. The bars group differences between miner-set timestamps in block height order.

Source: Blockchain.com Nov. 26 header records · Blockchain.com previous-day parent · Blockstream cross-check

A miner earns a chance at the block reward by finding a valid block whose header hash, computed by applying SHA-256 twice, is at or below the network target. How quickly a machine can sign for a test key leaves the cost of that search open.

A credible mining result would report repeated trials on fresh block templates against named models of specialized mining hardware, known as ASICs, at the same target. How many valid blocks does each setup produce per hour? How much energy or total cost goes into each expected accepted block, including work lost when another miner gets there first? Robert R. Nerem and Daya R. Gaur studied how the cost comparison might work for a small quantum miner competing with classical miners.

A cost advantage can matter commercially before a miner can deploy enough capacity to affect the network. Bitcoin nodes still independently check the transactions inside the blocks against the network’s spending rules.

#4993. Bitcoin Falls Further as Inflation, Trump Tariffs and AI Selloff Rattle Markets

Bitcoin Falls Further as Inflation, Trump Tariffs and AI Selloff Rattle Markets

Bitcoin fell below $58,000 Wednesday morning as stronger-than-expected U.S. economic growth, rising inflation and a fresh round of proposed tariffs from President Donald Trump's administration gave investors more reasons to sell.

The Nasdaq Composite dropped 4.3%, the S&P 500 lost 3%, and Nvidia shed 8.7% as of 9:50 a.m. ET. Bitcoin hit a session low of $57,500 as the selloff on Wall Street spilled over into the crypto market.

Paradoxically, part of the problem is that the U.S. economy is doing better than expected. The Bureau of Economic Analysis revised its estimate of third-quarter GDP growth from 3.4% to 4.3% at an annualized rate, nearly double the 2.2% recorded in the second quarter.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Bitcoin with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

But the Federal Reserve's preferred inflation gauge, the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index, rose 3.8% year-over-year in October, up from 3.6% in September and matching a three-year high set in May. Core PCE, which excludes food and energy prices, rose 3.3%, compared with economists' expectations of 3.2% and September's reading of 3.1%.

“America's inflation problem is bigger than an energy shock,” Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union, told AFP. Consumer spending increased in dollar terms in October but was flat after adjusting for inflation.

A growing economy gives the Fed more room to raise borrowing costs to bring inflation back toward its 2% target. After Wednesday's inflation release, traders were pricing in a 98% probability of a quarter-point increase in December, according to CME FedWatch data. Today odds are set at 94%.

The Fed held rates at between 3.75% and 4% in October after raising them in September for the first time in three years. Traders are also betting on further tightening in 2027, with another increase expected as early as January.

The Office of the U.S. Trade Representative proposed tariffs targeting 14 economies, including China, the European Union, Japan and South Korea, following investigations into government policies that encourage manufacturing production beyond market demand.

The proposed rates vary by country and product, with duties of up to 20% on some Chinese imports and up to 35% on Vietnamese goods, subject to adjustments and exemptions. For the EU, the proposed 15% rate accounts for certain existing duties rather than simply adding 15 percentage points to them.

The tariffs have not taken effect, and public hearings are scheduled to begin January 25. If importers pass the additional costs on to consumers, the duties could make the Fed's job of bringing inflation down even harder.

Meanwhile, Wall Street's enthusiasm over Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia didn't last very long. The chipmaker closed Monday up 31.5% but lost more than 6% Tuesday, while Anthropic closed at $81.91, below its $83 initial public offering price less than a week after its Nasdaq debut.

Higher interest rates make it more expensive to finance data centers and reduce the present value of future earnings. Both are particularly relevant for AI companies spending heavily today in anticipation of profits years down the road.

The selloff began well before Wall Street opened. South Korea's Kospi closed 6.16% lower, while spot gold fell 2% to $3,483.59 an ounce by 9:15 a.m. ET, according to Reuters.

Crypto investors were already in bad shape before Wednesday's economic data came out. Blockchain analytics firm Glassnode reported Tuesday that Bitcoin investors were realizing their heaviest losses since the collapse of FTX and the subsequent market crash in November 2022, relative to the money that flowed into the asset over the preceding year.

U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs have also recorded $4.94 billion in net outflows this November through Tuesday, according to Decrypt’s ETF tracker, already making it their worst month since launching in January 2024.

The Fed's next interest rate decision is scheduled for December 9.
